#### Recollection B.2.

Fix the same localization $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}$ of $\mathbf{Z}$ as in Assumption B.1. If $X$ is a closed oriented $n$ -manifold, the homology $\mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}X;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}):=\Sigma^{n}C_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}X;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ admits the structure of an algebra via the Chas-Sullivan product. This product is given by push-pull along the span $\mathcal{L}X\times\mathcal{L}X\leftarrow\mathrm{Map}(S^{1}\vee S^{1},X)\to\mathcal{L}X$ . If $X=G/H$ , one can identify

$$ \mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}X;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})=C_{\ast}(\Omega X;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})^{hH}\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}^{{}^{\prime}hG}}\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}. $$

Up to completion, $\mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}X;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ can be identified with the Hochschild cohomology $\mathrm{HC}(C^{\ast}(X;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})/\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ ; in particular, $\mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}X;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ is naturally an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ - $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}$ -algebra by the Deligne conjecture. See [BR, Theorem 1.0.2]. If $X$ is simply-connected, one can also view $\mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}X;\mathbf{Z})$ as the symplectic cohomology $\mathrm{SH}(T^{\ast}X;\mathbf{Z})$ by Viterbo’s theorem (see [Abo]).

Of course, the reader only interested in string topology with rational coefficients need not use Assumption B.1 in any of this discussion.

#### Theorem B.3.

Fix a spherical subgroup $H\subseteq G$ . Let $X\simeq(G/H)(\mathbf{C})$ denote the associated compact homogeneous manifold for the maximal compact subgroup of $G(\mathbf{C})$ . Under Assumption B.1, let

$$ {\check{{J}}}_{X}^{\prime}={\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}\times_{{\check{{M}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}/{\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}(-2\rho)}{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}, $$

so that there is a canonical morphism ${\check{{J}}}_{X}^{\prime}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}$ , and hence a canonical composite

$$ {\check{{J}}}_{X}^{\prime}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}. $$

Then there is an equivalence

$$ \mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}X;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})\simeq\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\Gamma\left({\check{{J}}}_{X}^{\prime}\times_{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}}\{0\};\mathcal{O}\right). $$

#### Proof.

It follows from Assumption B.1(b) and (an integral variant of) Theorem 3.6.4 that $\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}{\check{{J}}}_{X}^{\prime}\simeq\spec C^{H}_{\ast}(\Omega X;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ , so that

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}{\check{{J}}}_{X}^{\prime}\times_{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}}\{0\} \displaystyle\simeq\spec\left(C^{H}_{\ast}(\Omega X;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})\otimes_{C_{G}^{\ast}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})}\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}\right) \displaystyle\simeq\spec\left(C_{\ast}(\Omega X;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})^{hH}\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}^{{}^{\prime}hG}}\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}\right), $$

whose ring of functions identifies with $\mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}X;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ . ∎

Note that the full strength of Assumption B.1 is not really necessary; all one needs is an integral and derived refinement of the isomorphism ${\check{{J}}}_{X}^{\prime}\simeq\spec\mathrm{H}^{H}_{\ast}(\Omega X;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ from Theorem 3.6.4.

#### Remark B.4.

Combined with Theorem 3.6.4, Theorem B.3 says that if $G/H$ is simply-connected, one could view

$$ \mathrm{H}^{H}_{\ast}(\Omega(G/H);\mathbf{Z})\cong\mathrm{SH}_{G}^{\ast}(T^{\ast}(G/H);\mathbf{Z}), $$

the latter being some appropriate version of $G$ -equivariant symplectic cohomology (i.e., a $G$ -equivariant analogue of the string topology algebra $\mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}(G/H);\mathbf{Z})$ ). In particular, there should be a map of algebras

$$ \mathrm{H}^{G}_{\ast}(\Omega G;\mathbf{Z})\to\mathrm{SH}_{G}^{\ast}(T^{\ast}(G/H);\mathbf{Z}) $$

which is “coisotropic” as explained in Observation 5.2.11. See [GMP] for such a construction with coefficients in $\mathbf{C}$ . There should also be an equivalence (motivated by Theorem 3.6.4)

$$ \spec\mathrm{SH}_{G}^{\ast}(T^{\ast}(G/H);\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})\cong{\check{{J}}}_{X}^{\prime}. $$

Moreover, the isomorphism B.1 should hold much more generally with ordinary homology replaced by equivariant (connective) K-theory or equivariant elliptic cohomology, and equivariant symplectic cohomology replaced by the appropriate variant.

#### Example B.5 (Group case).

Suppose $G=H\times H$ , with $H$ embedded diagonally. Then $X$ is the maximal compact subgroup of $H(\mathbf{C})$ , so we will simply write $X=H$ for notational simplicity. We will also omit grading shifts. In this case, ${\check{{M}}}=T^{\ast}{\check{{H}}}$ . Assume a version of Theorem 3.2.7 with $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}$ coefficients. Then Theorem B.3 says that there is an equivalence

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}H;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}) \displaystyle\simeq\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\Gamma\left({\check{{J}}}_{{\check{{H}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}}\times_{{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}\times{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}}\{0\};\mathcal{O}\right) \displaystyle\simeq\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\Gamma\left(\left({\check{{J}}}_{{\check{{H}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}}\times_{{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}}\{0\}\right)\times\left(\{0\}\times_{{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}}\{0\}\right);\mathcal{O}\right) \displaystyle\simeq\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\Gamma\left(Z_{e}({\check{{H}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}})(-2\rho)\times({\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}})[-1];\mathcal{O}\right) $$

The final term is simply the shearing of the tensor product of $\mathcal{O}_{Z_{e}({\check{{H}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}})(-2\rho)}\cong\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\Omega H;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ (this isomorphism being provided by Proposition 5.4.1 and Remark 5.4.4) with an exterior algebra (which identifies with $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(H;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ by the theory of the Kostant slice). One therefore recovers [Hep, Theorem 1], which identifies $\pi_{\ast}\mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}H;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ with $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\Omega H;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})\otimes\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(H;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ .

Theorem B.3 also says that the calculations in Section 4 can be used to recover the calculations of [CJY], and more generally of the string topology of compact Riemannian symmetric spaces $X$ of rank one. For simplicity, we will assume $X$ is simply-connected, so $X$ is $S^{n}$ , ${\mathbf{C}P}^{n}$ , $\mathbf{H}P^{n}$ , or $\mathbf{O}P^{2}$ . These cases fall under the purview of the following lemma.

#### Lemma B.6.

Let $\mathbf{Z}[x,b]/bx^{k}$ denote the graded ring with $x$ in weight $-2i$ and $b$ in weight $2j$ . Then the quotient $(\mathbf{Z}[x,b]/bx^{k})/x^{k+\ell}$ has homotopy groups given by

$$ \pi_{\ast}(\mathbf{Z}[x,b]/bx^{k})/x^{k+\ell}\cong\mathbf{Z}[x,b,\sigma(bx^{k+\ell})]/(x^{k+\ell},bx^{k},\sigma(bx^{k+\ell})^{2},x^{k}\sigma(bx^{k+\ell})), $$

where $\sigma(bx^{k+\ell})$ lives in weight $2(j-(k+\ell)i)$ and degree $1$ . In particular, there is a graded isomorphism

$$ \pi_{\ast}\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}(\mathbf{Z}[x,b]/bx^{k})/x^{k+\ell}\cong\mathbf{Z}[x,b,\sigma(bx^{k+\ell})]/(x^{k+\ell},bx^{k},\sigma(bx^{k+\ell})^{2},x^{k}\sigma(bx^{k+\ell})), $$

where $\sigma(bx^{k+\ell})$ lives in weight $2(j-(k+\ell)i)+1$ .

#### Proof.

Let $n\geq k+\ell$ ; then, $bx^{n}=(bx^{k})x^{n-k}=b(x^{n})$ admits two nullhomotopies in this quotient, so we obtain a class $\sigma(bx^{n})$ which lives in weight $2(j-ni)$ and degree $1$ ; this class lies in the Massey product/Toda bracket $\langle{x^{n-k},x^{k},b}\rangle$ . Note that $\sigma(bx^{n})=x^{n-k-\ell}\sigma(bx^{k+\ell})$ . The relation $x^{k+\ell}=0$ implies that $x^{n-k}=0$ for $n-k\geq k+\ell$ ; so $x^{k}\sigma(bx^{k+\ell})=0$ . ∎

#### Example B.7.

Let $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}=\mathbf{Z}[\tfrac{1}{2}]$ , let $G=\mathrm{SO}_{n+1}$ , and let $H=\mathrm{SO}_{n}$ . Using the calculations in the proof of Theorem 4.4.1 and Theorem 4.6.1 (or rather, its variant for $\mathrm{SO}_{n+1}/\mathrm{SO}_{n}$ ), we obtain isomorphisms

$$ \displaystyle{\check{{J}}}_{\mathrm{SO}_{n+1}/\mathrm{SO}_{n}} \displaystyle\cong\spec\mathrm{H}_{\ast}^{\mathrm{SO}_{n}}(\Omega S^{n};\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}) \displaystyle\cong\begin{cases}\spec\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}\left[p_{1},\cdots,p_{j},(a+a^{-1})^{2},\tfrac{(a-a^{-1})^{2}}{p_{j}},\tfrac{a^{2}-a^{-2}}{p_{j}^{1/2}}\right]&n=2j+1,\\
\spec\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[p_{1},\cdots,p_{j-1},c_{j},b]/bc_{j}&n=2j;\end{cases} $$

here, $a$ lives in weight $0$ , and $b$ lives in weight $4j-2$ . See also [Dev2, Remark B.4] for the first isomorphism. This scheme lives over ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}$ , and we find:

- • If $n=2j+1$ , the map ${\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}$ is given by the map

$$ \mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[p_{1},\cdots,p_{j},c_{j+1}]\to\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[p_{1},\cdots,p_{j}],\ c_{j+1}\mapsto 0. $$

It follows from Theorem B.3 that $\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}S^{2j+1};\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ $\displaystyle\simeq\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\left(\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}\left[p_{1},\cdots,p_{j},(a+a^{-1})^{2},\tfrac{(a-a^{-1})^{2}}{p_{j}},\tfrac{a^{2}-a^{-2}}{p_{j}^{1/2}}\right]\right)/(p_{1},\cdots,p_{j},c_{j+1})$ $\displaystyle\simeq\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\left(\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}\left[(a+a^{-1})^{2},\tfrac{(a-a^{-1})^{2}}{p_{j}},\tfrac{a^{2}-a^{-2}}{p_{j}^{1/2}}\right]\right)/(p_{j},c_{j+1}).$ Though this looks complicated, the relations simplify dramatically: we find that the homotopy of this algebra is simply

$$ \pi_{\ast}\mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}S^{2j+1};\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})\cong\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}\left[\tfrac{a^{2}-a^{-2}}{p_{j}^{1/2}},\sigma(c_{j+1})\right]/\sigma(c_{j+1})^{2}, $$

where $\tfrac{a^{2}-a^{-2}}{p_{j}^{1/2}}$ lives in weight $2j$ and $\sigma(c_{j+1})$ (coming from the two nullhomotopies of $c_{j+1}$ ) lives in weight $-2(j+1)+1=-2j-1$ . As expected, this is precisely [CJY, Theorem 2(1)].

- • If $n=2j$ , the map ${\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}$ is given by the map

$$ \mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[p_{1},\cdots,p_{j}]\to\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[p_{1},\cdots,p_{j-1},c_{j}],\ p_{j}\mapsto c_{j}^{2}. $$

It follows from Theorem B.3 that $\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}S^{2j};\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ $\displaystyle\simeq\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}(\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[p_{1},\cdots,p_{j-1},c_{j},b]/bc_{j})/(p_{1},\cdots,p_{j-1},c_{j}^{2})$ $\displaystyle\simeq\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}(\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[c_{j},b]/bc_{j})/c_{j}^{2}.$ It follows from Lemma B.6 that there is a graded isomorphism

$$ \pi_{\ast}\mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}S^{2j};\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})\cong\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[c_{j},b,\sigma(bc_{j}^{2})]/(bc_{j},c_{j}^{2},\sigma(bc_{j}^{2})^{2},c_{j}\sigma(bc_{j}^{2})), $$

where $\sigma(bc_{j}^{2})$ lives in weight $-1$ . This is precisely [CJY, Theorem 2(2)], as expected.

#### Example B.8.

Let $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}=\mathbf{Z}[\frac{1}{n+1}]$ . Using the calculations in the proof of (an integral version of) Theorem 4.3.1, we obtain isomorphisms

$$ \displaystyle{\check{{J}}}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{n+1}/\mathrm{GL}_{n}} \displaystyle\cong\spec\mathrm{H}_{\ast}^{\mathrm{GL}_{n}}(\Omega{\mathbf{C}P}^{n};\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}) \displaystyle\cong\spec\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[c_{1},\cdots,c_{n-1},c_{n},b]/bc_{n}. $$

Here, $b$ lives in weight $2n$ . This scheme lives over ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}$ . Taking its fiber over the origin kills the ideal $(c_{2},\cdots,c_{n-1},c_{1}^{n}-c_{n},c_{1}c_{n})$ . Note that $c_{1}c_{n}=c_{1}^{n+1}$ . It follows from Theorem B.3 and Lemma B.6 that there is a graded isomorphism

$$ \pi_{\ast}\mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}{\mathbf{C}P}^{n};\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})\cong\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[c_{1},b,\sigma(bc_{1}^{n+1})]/(bc_{1}^{n},c_{1}^{n+1},\sigma(bc_{1}^{n+1})^{2},c_{1}^{n}\sigma(bc_{1}^{n+1})), $$

where $\sigma(bc_{1}^{n+1})$ lives in weight $-1$ . As expected, this is [CJY, Theorem 3].

#### Remark B.9.

Lemma B.6 shows that using Theorem 4.5.1 and Theorem 4.7.1, one obtains graded isomorphisms

$$ \displaystyle\pi_{\ast}\mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}\mathbf{H}P^{n};\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}) \displaystyle\cong\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[p_{1},b,\sigma(bp_{1}^{n+1})]/(bp_{1}^{n},p_{1}^{n+1},\sigma(bp_{1}^{n+1})^{2},p_{1}^{n}\sigma(bp_{1}^{n+1})), \displaystyle\pi_{\ast}\mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}\mathbf{O}P^{2};\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}) \displaystyle\cong\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[p_{2},b,\sigma(bp_{2}^{3})]/(bp_{2}^{2},p_{2}^{3},\sigma(bp_{2}^{3})^{2},p_{2}^{2}\sigma(bp_{2}^{3})). $$

Here, $b$ lives in weight $4n+2$ in the first line, and in weight $22$ in the second line. In the first line, one can take $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}=\mathbf{Z}[\tfrac{1}{n+1}]$ ; and in the second line, one can take $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}=\mathbf{Z}[\tfrac{1}{3}]$ ; see [Yan].3434 34 These denominators precisely encode the “very good primes” for ${\check{{G}}}$ ; for instance, a prime $p$ is very good for $\mathrm{PGL}_{n+1}$ if $p\nmid(n+1)$ , and is very good for $\mathrm{F}_{4}$ if $p\nmid 3$ . If a prime $p$ is very good for ${\check{{G}}}$ , it admits a quasi-logarithm ${\check{{G}}}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}$ in the sense of [KV] (see [FN, Corollary 6.4]), which should imply that the usual statement of Theorem 3.2.7 holds with coefficients in $\mathbf{F}_{p}$ . See Remark 3.2.8.

## Appendix C Questions/further directions

The work presented in this article is clearly far from being a complete story. There are numerous questions left open by our discussion, of varying levels of difficulty. I hope that the discussion in this article is compelling enough to motivate further study of these problems.

Let us begin with some broad questions. First, some conceptual questions about the place of this story in mathematics and physics:

- (a) Having been raised a topologist, it is inspiring to see the appearance of unstable homotopy-theoretic structures in Table 3 (such as EHP sequences and Hopf fibrations). It suggests that there might be an unstable analogue of Expectation 5.3.13 (the latter is already not well-defined!) giving a spectral decomposition for “ $G$ -equivariant sheaves of spaces on $\Omega G$ ”. There are some indications that this might be possible, and many that it might be impossible — but it is perhaps better to be optimistic! This question seems exceptionally difficult, even in the simplest case of $G$ being trivial. In this case, one can interpret the question as asking for an analogue of the theory of synthetic spectra à la [Pst] for spaces/homotopy types/anima. Considerations from the theory of power operations suggests that one should replace the fpqc stack $\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}$ of groupoids classifying spin formal groups and isomorphisms between them by some sort of fpqc stack of categories classifying spin formal groups and homomorphisms (in particular, including isogenies) between them.

- (b) As mentioned in [Dev2, Heuristic B.5], an unpublished conjecture of Gaiotto (which I learned about from Nakajima) says that the Coulomb branch of $4$ d $\mathcal{N}=2$ pure gauge theory over $\mathbf{R}^{3}\times S^{1}$ with a generic choice of complex structure and gauge group $G$ can be modeled via the periodic $G$ -equivariant complex K-theory of $\Omega G$ . The calculations of this paper suggest that perhaps one can modify this proposal to use connective equivariant complex K-theory instead, and that the Bott class is related to the radius of the circle $S^{1}$ (see also Remark 5.1.15). The Bott class being sent to zero then might correspond to the degeneration of $4$ d $\mathcal{N}=2$ pure gauge theory into $3$ d $\mathcal{N}=4$ pure gauge theory. For instance, in Remark 3.5.21, we find that if $T=S^{1}$ (say), going from integral to $\mathrm{ku}$ -homology has the effect of deforming the relation $[p,a]=\hbar$ in the Weyl algebra of $\mathbf{G}_{a}=\spec\mathbf{Z}[a]$ over $\mathbf{Z}$ to the relation $[p,a]=\hbar(1+\beta ap)$ over $\mathbf{Z}[\beta]$ . (The symbol $p$ corresponds to $\tfrac{1}{a}x$ in Remark 3.5.21.) Does such a deformation have any precedence in physics? Here is a more optimistic question. Kapustin and Witten (among others) proposed viewing the derived geometric Satake equivalence of Theorem 3.2.7 as an equivalence of categories stemming from S-duality for $4$ d $\mathcal{N}=4$ gauge theory. Does Theorem 3.7.18 have any relationship to $5$ d maximally supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory compactified on a circle of finite radius (related to the Bott class $\beta$ )?

- (c) One glaring omission in this article is the study of equivariance for loop rotation on the topological/A-side; as explained in [NS, BBB+] via the $\Omega$ -deformation and [Dev2, Remark B.2], this corresponds to deformation quantizing the spectral/B-side. From one point of view, it can be described as the study of the homology of the operad ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}\rtimes S^{1}$ associated to rotations about a line inside $\mathbf{R}^{3}$ . Is there a good theory of quantizations of $\mathrm{ku}$ -Hamiltonian spaces (and a classification thereof)? Motivated by this, and considerations involving Frobenius-constant quantizations à la Bezrukavnikov-Kaledin [BK], we are planning to discuss the $\mathrm{U}(n)$ -equivariant cohomology of the ${\mathbf{E}_{{2n+1}}}$ -operad with arbitrary complex-oriented coefficients in a later article [Dev5]. This discussion is heavily motivated by [DM2] (in particular, [DM2, Section 4.4] can be regarded as the simplest case of this story, namely the case of tori). Part of the reason for not discussing loop rotation equivariance in this article is our reliance on Proposition 3.5.1, which inherently breaks the natural $S^{1}$ -action on the free loop space.

- (d) Prove Conjecture 3.5.11. In every example I have studied, the construction of the relevant Kostant slice $\kappa_{{\check{{M}}}}:{\check{{M}}}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\to{\check{{M}}}/{\check{{G}}}$ relies on classical invariant theory, and proving a unified statement would be very interesting and important. One interesting feature in the known examples is that the construction of such slices involves constructing a “stronger” slice ${\check{{M}}}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\to{\check{{M}}}$ . However, this depends on some noncanonical choices, i.e., the map ${\check{{M}}}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\to{\check{{M}}}$ is not canonical. It would therefore also be interesting to show that ${\check{{G}}}$ acts transitively on the set of all such slices ${\check{{M}}}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\to{\check{{M}}}$ (in other words, that such a slice, if it exists, is unique if we ask it to land in ${\check{{M}}}/{\check{{G}}}$ instead of ${\check{{M}}}$ ). For the usual Kostant slice ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}$ , this was shown in [FM].

- (e) Give an explanation for the observation in Remark 3.6.25.

- (f) Can one prove ramified versions of the local equivalences studied in this article? See Conjecture 3.4.14 for the analogue of [BZSV, Conjecture 7.5.1] with tame ramification.

- (g) In many calculations, one gets the sense that the condition of sphericity should not be crucial in relative geometric Langlands. For instance, the criteria (a) and (b) of Theorem 3.6.4 do not use sphericity of $H_{\mathbf{C}}\subseteq G_{\mathbf{C}}$ at all (and as in Remark 3.6.7, Example 3.6.13, and Conjecture 3.6.15, there should be many interesting examples of relative Langlands duality for non-spherical subgroups). One of the immediate difficulties encountered when working with non-spherical subgroups is that $G_{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{C}[\![t]\!])$ -orbits on $G_{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{C}(\!(t)\!))/H_{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{C}(\!(t)\!))$ are not parametrized by a discrete set; so it is hard to do “combinatorics”. Nevertheless, it would be interesting to collect other non-spherical examples satisfying conditions (a) and (b) of Theorem 3.6.4; a sufficient supply of examples might suggest a way to understand this generalization of relative Langlands duality.

- (h) In the proof (from [BF1]) of Theorem 3.2.7, many calculations can be reduced to the case of semisimple rank $1$ , essentially by localization on the affine space ${\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/W=\spec\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ . Is it possible to tackle Conjecture 3.4.12 for affine homogeneous spherical varieties of higher rank by reduction to the rank $1$ case (in which case Theorem 3.4.16 can be applied)? The technique of localization of spherical varieties, studied in [Lun, Kno3], should be crucial here.

- (i) Let $C_{2}$ be the cyclic group of order $2$ . In the case of symmetric spaces, Conjecture 3.4.12 should be closely related to $C_{2}$ -equivariant derived algebraic geometry as studied by Mike Hill and his collaborators (see, e.g., [Hil]). Let $\sigma$ denote the sign representation of $C_{2}$ on $\mathbf{R}$ , and let $\varrho=1+\sigma$ denote the regular representation of $C_{2}$ on $\mathbf{C}$ .3535 35 The notation is intended to distinguish this $C_{2}$ from the $\mathbf{Z}/2$ appearing elsewhere in this article, as well as $\varrho$ from the half-sum of positive roots (which is usually denoted $\rho$ ). On the topic of notation: it would have been great if $\varrho$ was used to denote the r(h)otation representation of $C_{2}$ (which is frequently denoted by $\lambda=2\sigma$ ), instead of the regular representation of $C_{2}$ . If $Y$ is a $C_{2}$ -space, let $\mathcal{L}^{\sigma}Y$ denote the space of maps $\mathrm{Map}(S^{\sigma},Y)$ equipped with its natural $C_{2}$ -action. Let $G$ be a connected compact Lie group, let $\theta$ be a conjugate-linear involution on $G_{\mathbf{C}}$ preserving $G$ , and let $G^{\theta}$ denote the maximal compact subgroup of the fixed subgroup $G_{\mathbf{C}}^{\theta}$ . Then, there is a $C_{2}$ -equivariant homotopy equivalence of orbispaces

$$ G\backslash\mathcal{L}^{\sigma}G/G\simeq\mathrm{Bun}_{(G,\theta)}({\mathbf{C}P}^{1}_{\mathbf{R}}), $$

which gives an equivalence

$$ (G\backslash\mathcal{L}^{\sigma}G/G)^{C_{2}}\simeq G\backslash\mathcal{L}(G/G^{\theta}). $$

Note that ${\mathbf{C}P}^{1}_{\mathbf{R}}=S^{\varrho}$ (which one can think of as the unit sphere in $\varrho\oplus\mathbf{R}=\sigma\oplus\mathbf{R}^{2}$ ) is the standard real structure on ${\mathbf{C}P}^{1}$ . Let $R$ denote a normed algebra in genuine $C_{2}$ -spectra, and let $\Phi^{C_{2}}R$ denote its geometric fixed points (for instance, if $R=\underline{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the constant Mackey functor, $\Phi^{C_{2}}R$ is the connective cover of the Tate construction $\mathbf{F}_{2}^{tS^{1}}\simeq\mathbf{Z}^{tC_{2}}$ ). We expect that there is an $\infty$ -category $\mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}(\mathrm{Bun}_{(G,\theta)}({\mathbf{C}P}^{1}_{\mathbf{R}});R)$ of “ $C_{2}$ -equivariant sheaves of $R$ -modules on $\mathrm{Bun}_{(G,\theta)}({\mathbf{C}P}^{1}_{\mathbf{R}})$ ”. This $\infty$ -category should satisfy an analogue of Theorem 3.2.7. Taking geometric fixed points (in some appropriate categorical sense) of this putative spectral decomposition of $\mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}(\mathrm{Bun}_{(G,\theta)}({\mathbf{C}P}^{1}_{\mathbf{R}});R)$ should produce an analogue/special case of Conjecture 3.4.12 which describes $\mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/G^{\theta}(\!(t)\!);\Phi^{C_{2}}R)$ . For instance, one can try to access $\mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/G^{\theta}(\!(t)\!);\Phi^{C_{2}}R)$ via an analogue of Smith theory. The case of $G=\mathrm{GL}_{n}$ equipped with the orthogonal involution, and $R=\underline{\mathbf{Z}}$ , is especially interesting, and we hope to study this question in future work. Developing this theory should lead to important interactions between geometric Langlands for symmetric spaces and $C_{2}$ -equivariant homotopy theory.

- (j) What is the underlying reason/broader context for the similarities evident in Table 3 between the dual varieties to the rank $1$ affine homogeneous varieties? In our story, these reflect the similitude between the based loop spaces of odd/even-dimensional spheres, but there are many other examples of such similarities in higher rank. We will address this question in future work; see Remark 4.1.5 for a brief comment. The recent article [Les] by Leslie is also concerned with this topic.

Some of the most important issues in this article on the topological/A-side come from defining well-behaved sheaf theories.

- (k) Verify Hypothesis 3.5.2, and more generally Conjecture A.6.

- (l) Let $G$ be a compact Lie group, and let $X$ be an (ind-)finite stratified $G$ -space. Is there a good $\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\mathbf{Z}[\beta]$ -linear $\infty$ -category $\mathrm{Shv}_{G}^{c}(X;\mathrm{ku})$ which agrees with the ad hoc construction of Construction 3.7.15?

- (m) Is there a good sheaf theory of synthetic $G$ -equivariant constructible sheaves of spectra as in Expectation 5.3.10? As a first step, it seems important to study $G$ -equivariant analogues of synthetic spectra, as well as nonequivariant synthetic analogues of constructible sheaves of spectra.

The discussion in this article also suggests several (less lofty, and presumably more approachable) questions.

- (n) Can one define ${\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{univ}}}$ as in Expectation 5.3.11?

- (o) Is there an a priori reason that if ${\check{{M}}}_{\beta}$ is an ${\check{{G}}}$ -variety over $\mathbf{Z}[\beta]$ as in Proposition 3.7.20, the map ${\check{{M}}}_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}}\to{\check{{G}}}^{\mathrm{sc}}_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}}$ admits a Lagrangian structure? See Observation 5.2.11 for some progress in this direction.

- (p) As in Remark 3.5.19, let $W_{1}\to W_{2}$ be a homomorphism of reflection groups acting on vector spaces $V_{1}\to V_{2}$ over a field $k$ (possibly of nonzero characteristic), so that there is a map $V_{1}/\!\!/W_{1}\to V_{2}/\!\!/W_{2}$ . The Hochschild homology $\mathrm{HH}(V_{1}/\!\!/W_{1}/V_{2}/\!\!/W_{2})$ should be an interesting invariant associated to homomorphisms of reflection groups; what can one prove about it? In the case that the map of reflection groups comes from an inclusion of root data, this Hochschild homology is the content of Proposition 3.5.7, and therefore plays an important role in the relative Langlands program.

- (q) Is there an analogue of Theorem 4.6.1 for $\mathrm{ku}$ ? The difficulty lies in finding a $\beta$ -deformation of ${\check{{M}}}$ .

- (r) Can one extend Theorem 3.7.18 to the non-simply-laced case? Similarly, can one extend Proposition 5.4.1 to coefficients with the sphere spectrum? Following Lemma 5.4.10, a first step will be an understanding of $\mathrm{MU}_{\ast}(\Omega G)$ as a Hopf algebra; the cobordism groups are known by [Pet]. A description of the $\mathrm{MU}_{\ast}\mathrm{MU}$ -comodule structure would then give the desired generalization of Proposition 5.4.1.

- (s) Fix a prime $p$ . Can the results of this article (even only the ones concerning coefficients in ordinary commutative rings) be extended to the setting of $p$ -compact groups? This question was suggested by Haynes Miller. See [Gro] for a survey of the theory of $p$ -compact groups. Let us make some brief comments about this question. First, if the input into the machinery of geometric Langlands duality is the $p$ -completion of a compact torus $T$ , the “Langlands dual” appears to be the $p$ -divisible subgroup ${\check{{T}}}[p^{\infty}]$ of the Langlands dual torus ${\check{{T}}}$ . (In the rank one case, this reduces to the statement that the Cartier dual of $\Omega(S^{1})^{\wedge}_{p}=\mathbf{Z}_{p}$ , if interpreted suitably, is $\mu_{p^{\infty}}$ .) Second, the simplest exotic case of the Sullivan sphere $(S^{2n-1})^{\wedge}_{p}=\Omega(B^{2}\mathbf{Z}_{p})_{h{\mathbf{Z}/n}}$ for $n|\#\mathbf{F}_{p}^{\times}$ , which behaves like a compact Lie group of rank $1$ , already seems to exhibit an interesting Langlands duality: its “dual group” is built out of the $p$ -divisible torus $\mu_{p^{\infty}}$ and the Weyl group ${\mathbf{Z}/n}$ acting via ${\mathbf{Z}/n}\subseteq\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{\times}\circlearrowright\mu_{p^{\infty}}$ . Third, in [Dev4, Remark 3.13], I suggest that the Dwyer-Wilkerson exotic $2$ -compact group from [DW] might act on a framed $30$ -manifold with Kervaire invariant $1$ (just as $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ acts on $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\times 3}/\mathrm{PGL}_{2}\cong\mathbf{R}P^{3}\times\mathbf{R}P^{3}$ and $\mathrm{G}_{2}$ acts on $\mathrm{SO}_{8}/\mu_{2}\cdot\mathrm{G}_{2}\cong\mathbf{R}P^{7}\times\mathbf{R}P^{7}$ ), and that the “regular centralizer” group scheme for this action should be related to the relative Langlands program. See [Dev4] for (brief) further discussion.

- (t) Finding other examples of the $\mathrm{ku}$ -theoretic analogue of [BZSV, Conjecture 7.5.1] is an important goal. For instance, what is the $\mathrm{ku}$ -theoretic dual of the spherical $\mathrm{GL}_{n}$ -variety $\mathrm{GL}_{n}/(\mathrm{GL}_{j}\times\mathrm{GL}_{n-j})$ (which is homotopy equivalent to $\mathrm{Gr}_{j}(\mathbf{C}^{n})$ )? In the arithmetic case, this was studied by Jacquet-Rallis in [JR], and is described in Conjecture 3.6.15 in the geometric case.

- (u) Is there an analogue of the theory of synthetic spectra for global homotopy theory?

- (v) Is there a structure theory for $\mathrm{ku}$ -Hamiltonian spaces? Namely, is there a well-behaved theory of “hyperspherical” $\mathrm{ku}$ -Hamiltonian spaces which generalizes the notion of hyperspherical Hamiltonian spaces introduced in [BZSV, Section 3], and an analogue of [BZSV, Theorem 3.6.1]?

- (w) Related to the preceding point, can one develop a theory of $\beta$ -deformed cotangent bundles for certain $G$ -varieties? In the case of “coisotropic subgroups” as in Remark 5.1.20, this would be a $\beta$ -deformation of [BM] (or rather, of the specialization of their results to quasi-Hamiltonian spaces).

# Derived geometric Satake for $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\times 3}/\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\mathrm{diag}}$ Thanks: Part of this work was done when the author was supported by NSF DGE-2140743

**Authors:** S. K. Devalapurkar Address: 1 Oxford St, Cambridge, MA 02139 Email address: sdevalapurkar@math.harvard.edu, August 24, 2026

## Abstract

In this note, we study the local relative geometric Langlands conjecture of Ben-Zvi–Sakellaridis–Venkatesh for the spherical subgroup $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\mathrm{diag}}$ of the triple product $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\times 3}$ (and also for the spherical subgroup $\mathrm{G}_{2}$ of $\mathrm{SO}_{8}/\mu_{2}$ ), whose corresponding Langlands dual $\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 3}$ -variety can be identified with the symplectic vector space $(\mathbf{A}^{2})^{\otimes 3}\cong\mathbf{A}^{8}$ of $2\times 2\times 2$ -cubes. Our analysis relies on a construction of Bhargava relating $2\times 2\times 2$ -cubes to Gauss composition on quadratic forms, arising here as the moment map for the Hamiltonian $\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 3}$ -action on $(\mathbf{A}^{2})^{\otimes 3}$ , and the Cayley hyperdeterminant as studied by Gelfand-Kapranov-Zelevinsky.

#### Contents

- 1 Introduction

- 2 Some properties of $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}$

- 3 The proof, and some remarks

- 4 Variants

- References

## 1. Introduction

The goal of this brief note is to study the geometrization of a story from the arithmetic context pioneered by Böcherer, Gross, Harris, Ichino, Kudla, Prasad, Schulze-Pillot, and Watson, among many others (see, e.g., [HK, Ich, Pra, Wat]): this tale is about the “triple product period”. In the language of geometric representation theory, our goal is to study derived geometric Satake ([BZSV, Conjecture 7.5.1]) for the spherical $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\times 3}$ -variety $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\times 3}/\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\mathrm{diag}}$ . This is a natural generalization of the “group case”, i.e., derived geometric Satake for the spherical $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\times 2}$ -variety $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\times 2}/\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\mathrm{diag}}$ (which amounts simply to the derived geometric Satake equivalence of [BF] for $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ ). Similar methods allow us to analyze the spherical $\mathrm{PSO}_{8}$ -variety $\mathrm{PSO}_{8}/\mathrm{G}_{2}$ , too. In order to state our main result, some notation is necessary.

#### Notation 1.1.

Let $\mathrm{std}$ denote the standard representation of $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ , so that $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}$ consists of cubes

$$ \textstyle{b_{2}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{d_{3}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{a\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{b_{1}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{d_{1}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{c.} \textstyle{b_{3}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{d_{2}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} $$

Fix an integer $n$ . Equip $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}$ with the grading where the entries of a cube have the following weights: $a$ lives in weight $-4n$ , each $b_{i}$ lives in weight $-2n$ , $c$ lives in weight $2n$ , and each $d_{i}$ lives in weight $0$ . Write $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}(4n,\vec{2n},-2n,\vec{0})$ to denote the corresponding graded variety.

Similarly, equip $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ with the grading where the entries of a matrix $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}$ have the following weights: $a$ and $d$ live in weight $0$ , $b$ lives in weight $2n$ , and $c$ lives in weight $-2n$ . Write $\mathrm{SL}_{2}(-2n\rho)$ to denote this graded group. Then there is a natural graded action of $\mathrm{SL}_{2}(-2n\rho)^{\times 3}$ on $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}(4n,\vec{2n},-2n,\vec{0})$ .

Recall that the process of shearing (denoted $\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}$ ) discussed in [Rak, Lur], as well as [Dev, Section 2.1], converts gradings into homological shifts (more precisely, it sends a module in weight $n$ to the same module shifted homologically by $n$ ). This functor is symmetric monoidal when restricted to the subcategory of modules in even weights, and therefore extends to an operation on evenly graded stacks. If $Y$ is a graded stack, let $\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}Y$ denote the corresponding derived stack obtained by shearing, and let $\mathrm{Perf}^{\mathrm{sh}}(Y)$ denote $\mathrm{Perf}(\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}Y)$ . Almost all of our discussion below takes place in the setting of ordinary, and not derived, algebraic geometry, and so the reader unfamiliar with derived algebraic geometry should feel free to ignore this procedure of shearing.11 1 The reader intent on ignoring shearing might feel some solace in noting that our main results should continue to hold with the $\infty$ -category of constructible sheaves replaced by a mixed variant. However, this must (hopefully temporarily) be regarded as a reverie, since no “mixed” version of the derived geometric Satake equivalence seems to exist in the literature.

As in [Dev], we will state all of our results with “arithmetic shearing” in the sense of [BZSV, Section 6.7]. The following result concerns [BZSV, Conjecture 7.5.1] for the Hamiltonian $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\times 3}$ -variety $T^{\ast}(\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\times 3}/\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\mathrm{diag}})$ and the Hamiltonian $\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 3}$ -variety $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}$ .

#### Theorem 1.2 (Derived geometric Satake for $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\times 3}/\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\mathrm{diag}}$ ).

Suppose that the $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\times 3}[\![t]\!]$ -action on $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\times 3}(\!(t)\!)/\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\mathrm{diag}}(\!(t)\!)$ is optimal in the sense of [Dev, Hypothesis 3.5.2]. There is an equivalence22 2 The $\infty$ -category on the left-hand side is as in [Dev, Definition 3.6.1]; see Definition 3.1 for a quick review.

$$ \mathrm{Shv}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\times 3}[\![t]\!]}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}(\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\times 3}(\!(t)\!)/\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\mathrm{diag}}(\!(t)\!));\mathbf{Q})\simeq\mathrm{Perf}^{\mathrm{sh}}(\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}(4,\vec{2},-2,\vec{0})/\mathrm{SL}_{2}(-2\rho)^{\times 3}). $$

Moreover, this equivalence is equivariant for the action of the spherical Hecke category for $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\times 3}$ ; on the spectral side, this action is encoded by Bhargava’s construction $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}\to\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast,\times 3}$ of three quadratic forms from a point of $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}$ (see [Bha1, Woo]).

#### Remark 1.3.

The hypothesis of optimality in Theorem 1.2 is equivalent to the hypothesis that the diagonal action of $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}[\![t]\!]$ on $\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}}\times\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}}$ is optimal, where $\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}}$ is the affine Grassmannian of $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ . In particular, [Dev, Hypothesis 3.5.2(a) and (b)] can be deduced from this observation. Checking purity of the $\mathrm{IC}$ -sheaves seems a bit trickier, but should not be difficult.

#### Remark 1.4.

Let $\mathrm{PSO}_{2n}:=\mathrm{SO}_{2n}/\mu_{2}$ . Then, the embedding $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\mathrm{diag}}\subseteq\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\times 3}$ can be identified with the diagonal embedding $\mathrm{SO}_{3}\subseteq\mathrm{SO}_{3}\times\mathrm{PSO}_{4}$ ; and similarly, the action of $\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 3}$ on $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}$ can be identified with the action of $\mathrm{Spin}_{4}\times\mathrm{Sp}_{2}$ on the tensor product of their respective defining representations. From this perspective, Theorem 1.2 could be viewed as a special case of the geometrized analogue of the Gan-Gross-Prasad period (or at least a period isogenous to it). See Remark 3.12 (as well as [Dev, Example 3.6.24]) for a discussion of the Gan-Gross-Prasad period along the lines of this article.

See Remark 3.10 for an analogue of Theorem 1.2 for the non-spherical variety $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\times 4}/\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\mathrm{diag}}$ .

An argument similar to that of Theorem 1.2 shows a variant for $\mathrm{PSO}_{8}$ . (The arithmetic version of the result stated below was studied, for instance, in [Jia2, Jia3].) Namely, there is an embedding $\mathrm{G}_{2}\subseteq\mathrm{PSO}_{8}$ given by triality, which exhibits $\mathrm{G}_{2}$ as a spherical subgroup of $\mathrm{PSO}_{8}$ . To see that this situation is analogous to that of Theorem 1.2, note that the Dynkin diagram $\bullet$ of $A_{1}$ is obtained from the Dynkin diagram $\bullet\bullet\bullet$ of $A_{1}^{\times 3}$ by folding with respect to the obvious action of the symmetric group $\Sigma_{3}$ . In the same way, the Dynkin diagram of $\mathrm{G}_{2}$ is obtained from the Dynkin diagram of $D_{4}$ by folding with respect to the action of $\Sigma_{3}$ permuting the three vertices around the branching vertex. The following result concerns [BZSV, Conjecture 7.5.1] for the Hamiltonian $\mathrm{PSO}_{8}$ -variety $T^{\ast}(\mathrm{PSO}_{8}/\mathrm{G}_{2})$ and the Hamiltonian $\mathrm{Spin}_{8}$ -variety $\mathrm{Ind}_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 3}}^{\mathrm{Spin}_{8}}(\mathbf{A}^{1}\oplus\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3})$ .

#### Theorem 1.5 (Derived geometric Satake for $\mathrm{PSO}_{8}/\mathrm{G}_{2}$ ).

Suppose that the $\mathrm{PSO}_{8}[\![t]\!]$ -action on $\mathrm{PSO}_{8}(\!(t)\!)/\mathrm{G}_{2}(\!(t)\!)$ is optimal in the sense of [Dev, Hypothesis 3.5.2]. Then there is an equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Shv}_{\mathrm{PSO}_{8}[\![t]\!]}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}(\mathrm{PSO}_{8}(\!(t)\!)/\mathrm{G}_{2}(\!(t)\!);\mathbf{Q})\simeq\mathrm{Perf}^{\mathrm{sh}}(\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}(12,\vec{6},-6,\vec{0})/\mathrm{SL}_{2}(-6\rho)^{\times 3}\times\mathbf{A}^{1}(4)). $$

This implies, for instance, that the spherical subgroups $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\times 2}\subseteq\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\times 4}$ (given by $(g,h)\mapsto(g,g,g,h)$ ) and $\mathrm{G}_{2}\subseteq\mathrm{PSO}_{8}$ have the same dual quotient stacks (namely, $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}/\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 3}\times\mathbf{A}^{1}$ ) up to grading. Therefore, they fit into the paradigm of [Dev, Remark 4.1.5].

The proofs of Theorem 1.2 and Theorem 1.5 reduce to showing that the conditions of [Dev, Theorem 3.6.4] are met. This ultimately relies on studying Bhargava’s construction from [Bha1] relating $2\times 2\times 2$ -matrices to quadratic forms, and the work [GKZ] of Gelfand-Kapranov-Zelevinsky describing the relationship to Cayley’s hyperdeterminant. The work presented in this article indicates that there is much more to explore regarding the relationship between (relative) geometric Langlands (following [BZSV]), prehomogeneous vector spaces (following [SK]), and the progress in arithmetic invariant theory (using the terminology of [BG]) over the past 20 years spurred by Bhargava’s thesis. To illustrate this, here are two concrete questions in the interface of these subjects:

- • Can one use Bhargava’s work [Bha1] on the $\mathrm{SL}_{6}(\mathbf{Z})$ -action on $\wedge^{3}\mathbf{Z}^{6}$ to approach the geometrized version of [GR1] (i.e., [BZSV, Line 16 of Table 1.5.1])? (Here, the information flows from arithmetic invariant theory to relative geometric Langlands.)

- • Following the work of Moore and Tachikawa in [MT], let $\overline{\mathcal{O}}:=\overline{\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{min}}}(\mathfrak{so}_{8})$ denote the minimal nilpotent coadjoint orbit of $\mathfrak{so}_{8}$ , so that it is $10$ -dimensional. It has a canonical action of $\mathrm{SO}_{8}$ , and hence a canonical action of $\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 4}\subseteq\mathrm{SO}_{8}$ . In fact, more is true: there is an action of the symmetric group $\Sigma_{4}$ on $\mathfrak{so}_{8}$ extending the $\Sigma_{3}\subseteq\Sigma_{4}$ -action by triality, whose fixed subgroup is $\mathfrak{sl}_{3}\subseteq\mathfrak{g}_{2}$ . (See [FJLS, Section 4.1] for a description of this action.) This defines an action of $\Sigma_{4}$ on $\overline{\mathcal{O}}$ , and in fact the action of $\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 4}$ on $\overline{\mathcal{O}}$ is $\Sigma_{4}$ -equivariant for the permutation action on $\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 4}$ . The action $\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 4}\circlearrowleft\overline{\mathcal{O}}$ should be viewed as the analogue of $\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 3}\circlearrowleft(\mathbf{A}^{2})^{\otimes 3}$ ; see also Remark 3.10.33 3 Here is another (related) reason. As described in [Dev, Remark 3.6.25], both of these examples can be placed in the following context. The groups $(\mathrm{SL}_{2},\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 2})$ form a reductive dual pair in $\mathrm{Sp}_{8}$ , and $(\mathbf{A}^{2})^{\otimes 3}$ is a double cover of the minimal nilpotent orbit closure of $\mathrm{Sp}_{8}$ . Similarly, the groups $(\mathrm{SL}_{2},\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 3})$ form a reductive dual pair in $\mathrm{SO}_{8}$ , and $\overline{\mathcal{O}}$ is the minimal nilpotent orbit closure of $\mathrm{SO}_{8}$ . One should therefore view these examples as falling under the purview of Howe duality. There is a map $\overline{\mathcal{O}}\to\mathbf{A}^{1}$ , which we will call the “discriminant”, which defines an isomorphism

$$ \overline{\mathcal{O}}/\!\!/\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 4}\xrightarrow{{\sim}}\mathbf{A}^{1}, $$

at least over $\mathbf{C}$ . The above isomorphism should also hold true over $\mathbf{Z}$ . Following [Bha1], let us introduce some terminology. An ordered tuple $(I_{1},I_{2},I_{3},I_{4})$ of oriented ideals of a quadratic ring $S$ such that $I_{1}I_{2}I_{3}I_{4}\subseteq S$ and $N(I_{1})N(I_{2})N(I_{3})N(I_{4})=1$ will be called balanced, and say that two such balanced tuples $(I_{1},I_{2},I_{3},I_{4})$ and $(I_{1}^{\prime},I_{2}^{\prime},I_{3}^{\prime},I_{4}^{\prime})$ are equivalent if there are elements $x_{1},\cdots,x_{4}\in S\otimes\mathbf{Q}$ such that $I_{j}^{\prime}=x_{j}I_{j}$ . Say that an $\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 4}(\mathbf{Z})$ -orbit on $\overline{\mathcal{O}}(\mathbf{Z})$ is nondegenerate if its discriminant is nonzero. Then, one should have the following analogue of [Bha1, Theorem 11]: Conjecture 1.6. There is a canonical bijection between the set of nondegenerate $\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 4}(\mathbf{Z})$ -orbits on $\overline{\mathcal{O}}(\mathbf{Z})$ and the set of isomorphism classes of pairs $(S,(I_{1},I_{2},I_{3},I_{4}))$ of a nondegenerate oriented quadratic ring $S$ and an equivalence class $(I_{1},I_{2},I_{3},I_{4})$ of balanced oriented ideals of $S$ . If this were true, one could symmetrize, i.e., take $I_{1}=I_{2}=I_{3}=I_{4}$ , so that $I:=I_{1}$ will be a $4$ -torsion element in the class group of $S$ . It would be very interesting if one could use the explicit description of the invariant quotient $\overline{\mathcal{O}}/\!\!/\Sigma_{4}$ in [FJLS, Theorem 4.6 and Theorem 4.12] to describe the asymptotics of $4$ -torsion in class groups of quadratic rings over $\mathbf{Z}$ . (Here, the information flows from relative geometric Langlands to arithmetic invariant theory.)

In Remark 2.14 and Remark 4.14, I have included some further natural observations/questions whose role in the picture of geometric Langlands is unclear to me, in the hopes that it will stimulate further investigation into these questions.

#### Remark 1.7.

The arguments of this article should continue to hold if one considers sheaves with coefficients in $\mathbf{Z}[\frac{1}{2}]$ ; we have not checked this explicitly, but it seems likely to be true. In fact, we expect that the results of this article should continue to hold for sheaves with coefficients in $\mathbf{Z}$ itself. This, however, is a rather more subtle question: the prime $2$ is an interesting one (see Remark 2.8).

More generally, following the philosophy of [Dev], it should also be possible to use a variant of the methods of this article to prove analogues of Theorem 1.2 and Theorem 1.5 for sheaves with coefficients in connective complex K-theory $\mathrm{ku}$ . We have not attempted to do this, but we expect the corresponding $1$ -parameter deformation of $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}$ over $\pi_{\ast}(\mathrm{ku})\cong\mathbf{Z}[\beta]$ to be a rather interesting $\mathrm{ku}$ -Hamiltonian $\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 3}$ -variety.

#### Remark 1.8.

The equivalence of Theorem 1.2 can heuristically be viewed as geometric Langlands for $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ on the “doubled raviolo”, obtained by gluing three formal disks along their common punctured disk. I expect Theorem 1.2 to be related to the work of [MT], and hope to address this relationship and the context of Theorem 1.2 in physics in joint work with Ben-Zvi and Gunningham.

Theorem 1.2 is also related to the monoidality of the derived Satake equivalence. The $\infty$ -category $\mathrm{Shv}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\times 3}[\![t]\!]}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}(\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\times 3}(\!(t)\!)/\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\mathrm{diag}}(\!(t)\!));\mathbf{Q})$ can be identified with $\mathrm{Shv}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}[\![t]\!]}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}}\times\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}};\mathbf{Q})$ , where $\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}}$ is the affine Grassmannian of $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ . In particular, it can be used to describe the ordinary tensor product on $\mathrm{Shv}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}[\![t]\!]}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}};\mathbf{Q})$ . Theorem 1.2 says that under the derived geometric Satake equivalence of [BF] identifying this $\infty$ -category with $\mathrm{Perf}^{\mathrm{sh}}(\Sym^{2}(\mathrm{std})/\mathrm{SL}_{2})$ , the ordinary tensor product on $\mathrm{Shv}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}[\![t]\!]}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}};\mathbf{Q})$ can be identified with Gauss composition of binary quadratic forms (in the way described by Bhargava), i.e., via the correspondence 2.44 4 This is similar to how the convolution tensor product on $\mathrm{Shv}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}[\![t]\!]}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}};\mathbf{Q})$ can be identified with the usual tensor product on $\mathrm{Perf}^{\mathrm{sh}}(\Sym^{2}(\mathrm{std})/\mathrm{SL}_{2})$ . (In fact, I learned after writing this article that the main calculation of this article also appears in [BFN, Section 5(iii)]. The approach taken here is somewhat different, in that the calculations are more explicit and fit into the story of [Dev]; I hope that the reader might find this alternative perspective useful.)

In the final section of this article, we suggest some variants of Theorem 1.2 with $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\times 3}$ replaced by variants. Namely, we expect:

- • Let $G=\mathrm{Res}_{\mathbf{C}[\![t^{1/3}]\!]/\mathbf{C}[\![t]\!]}\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ , where $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ is viewed as a constant group scheme over $\mathbf{C}[\![t^{1/3}]\!]$ . Then there should be a fully faithful functor from the $\infty$ -category of perfect complexes on a shearing of the quotient stack $\Sym^{3}(\mathrm{std})/\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ to $\mathrm{Shv}_{G[\![t]\!]}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}(G(\!(t)\!)/\mathrm{PGL}_{2}(\!(t)\!);\mathbf{Q})$ . The grading with respect to which the shearing is taken is described in Conjecture 4.7.

- • Let $G=\mathrm{Res}_{(\mathbf{C}[\![t^{1/2}]\!]\times\mathbf{C}[\![t]\!])/\mathbf{C}[\![t]\!]}\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ . Then there should be a fully faithful functor from the $\infty$ -category of perfect complexes on a shearing of the quotient stack $(\mathrm{std}\otimes\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast})/\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 2}$ to $\mathrm{Shv}_{G[\![t]\!]}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}(G(\!(t)\!)/\mathrm{PGL}_{2}(\!(t)\!);\mathbf{Q})$ . The grading with respect to which the shearing is taken is described in Conjecture 4.11.

#### Remark 1.9.

The quotient stack $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}/\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 3}$ is also studied (in different language, of course) in quantum information theory; see Remark 2.11 below.

Theorem 1.2 and Theorem 1.5 are predicted by (the Betti version of) the local geometric conjecture of Ben-Zvi–Sakellaridis–Venkatesh; see [BZSV, Conjecture 7.5.1]. My homotopy-theoretic interpretation of their conjecture is as follows. Suppose $G$ is a reductive group over $\mathbf{C}$ and $G/H$ is an affine homogeneous spherical $G$ -variety (meaning that it admits an open $B$ -orbit for its natural left $B\subseteq G$ -action). Then, there should be a dual graded ${\check{{G}}}$ -variety ${\check{{M}}}$ equipped with a moment map $\mu:{\check{{M}}}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}$ , and an equivalence of the form

$$ \mathrm{Shv}_{G[\![t]\!]}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}(G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!);\mathbf{C})\simeq\mathrm{Perf}^{\mathrm{sh}}({\check{{M}}}/{\check{{G}}}), $$

where $\mathrm{Perf}^{\mathrm{sh}}$ denotes the $\infty$ -category of perfect complexes on the shearing of ${\check{{M}}}/{\check{{G}}}$ with respect to its given grading. In fact, [BZSV, Section 4] gives an explicit construction of this predicted dual ${\check{{M}}}$ , and in the examples $(G,H)=(\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\times 3},\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\mathrm{diag}})$ and $(\mathrm{PSO}_{8},\mathrm{G}_{2})$ , one can compute that the stacky quotient ${\check{{M}}}/{\check{{G}}}$ is isomorphic to the right-hand sides of Theorem 1.2 and Theorem 1.5 respectively.55 5 In the first case, this computation is straightforward given the prescription of [BZSV, Section 4]; see [Sak, Example 7.2.4] for a reference. The computation in the second case goes as follows. As in [BZSV, Remark 7.1.1], the quotient stack ${\check{{M}}}/{\check{{G}}}$ can be identified with the quotient ${\check{{V}}}_{X}/{\check{{G}}}_{X}$ , where ${\check{{G}}}_{X}$ is the Gaitsgory-Nadler/Sakellaridis-Venkatesh/Knop-Schalke dual group of $X$ and ${\check{{V}}}_{X}$ is constructed in [BZSV, Section 4.5]. In the case $X=\mathrm{PSO}_{8}/\mathrm{G}_{2}$ , a calculation shows that ${\check{{G}}}_{X}$ is the Levi subgroup of the maximal parabolic subgroup of $\mathrm{PSO}_{8}$ corresponding to the central vertex of the $D_{4}$ Dynkin diagram; so ${\check{{G}}}_{X}\cong\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 3}$ . Using the prescription of [BZSV, Section 4.5], one can check that ${\check{{V}}}_{X}\cong\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}\oplus\mathbf{A}^{1}$ , where ${\check{{G}}}_{X}$ acts only on the first factor. See, e.g., [Sak, Line 9 of Table in Appendix A].

Lest Theorem 1.2 seem like an oddly specific example to focus on, we note that it is essentially the only “new” example of a spherical pair $(G,H)$ of the form $(H^{\times j},H^{\mathrm{diag}})$ , as shown by the following lemma.

#### Lemma 1.10.

Suppose $H$ is a simple linear algebraic group over $\mathbf{C}$ . Then the subgroup $H^{\mathrm{diag}}\subseteq H^{\times j}$ is spherical if and only if:

- (a) $j=2$ , and $H$ arbitrary;

- (b) $j=3$ and $H$ is of type $A_{1}$ .

#### Proof.

If the subgroup $H^{\mathrm{diag}}\subseteq H^{\times j}$ is spherical, there is an open $H^{\mathrm{diag}}$ -orbit on the flag variety of $H^{\times j}$ . This implies that the dimension of $H$ must be at least $j|\Phi^{+}|$ , where $\Phi^{+}$ is the set of positive roots; equivalently, one needs $\mathrm{rank}(H)\geq(j-2)|\Phi^{+}|$ . Of course, this is always satisfied if $j=2$ (this is the group case corresponding to the symmetric subgroup $H^{\mathrm{diag}}\subseteq H\times H$ ). Using the classification of simple linear algebraic groups over $\mathbf{C}$ , it is easy to see that the only other case when the above inequality can hold is when $j=3$ and $H$ is of type $A_{1}$ ; one can then check by hand that the diagonal subgroup in this case is indeed spherical. ∎

In the first case of Lemma 1.10, [BZSV, Conjecture 7.5.1] is precisely the derived geometric Satake equivalence of [BF]. Therefore, the only other case of Lemma 1.10 is when $H$ is simple of type $A_{1}$ , and Theorem 1.2 precisely addresses [BZSV, Conjecture 7.5.1] for the adjoint form $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ of $H$ .

## 2. Some properties of $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}$

In this section, we establish some basic properties of $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}$ as a $\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 3}$ -variety; our base field will always be $\mathbf{Q}$ , and we will write ${\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 3}$ . Some of this material appears in [Bha1, Woo]. In particular, Construction 2.3 is due to Bhargava.

#### Observation 2.1.

An element $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&-a\end{pmatrix}\in\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast}\cong\mathfrak{sl}_{2}$ can be identified with a binary quadratic form $q_{A}(x,y)=cx^{2}+2axy-by^{2}$ . The resulting identification between $\Sym^{2}(\mathrm{std})=(\mathrm{std}\otimes\mathrm{std})_{\Sigma_{2}}$ and $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}$ is $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ -equivariant. Note, moreover, that the discriminant of $q_{A}(x,y)$ is $-4\mathrm{det}(A)$ .

#### Warning 2.2.

Note that under Observation 2.1, the element of $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast}$ associated to a binary quadratic form $bx^{2}+axy+cy^{2}$ is not the symmetric matrix associated to the quadratic form! Indeed, the associated symmetric matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}b&a/2\\ a/2&c\end{pmatrix}$ , while the associated element of $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast}$ is $\begin{pmatrix}a/2&c\\ b&-a/2\end{pmatrix}$ .

Note, also, that we are relying quite heavily on the assumption that $2$ is invertible in $\mathbf{Q}$ . Over $\mathbf{Z}$ , one can in fact identify the space $(\mathbf{A}^{2}\otimes\mathbf{A}^{2})_{\Sigma_{2}}$ of binary quadratic forms with the coadjoint representation $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast}\cong\mathfrak{pgl}_{2}$ of $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ . Working over $\mathbf{Z}$ and keeping track of the difference between $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}$ and $\mathfrak{pgl}_{2}$ has the effect of eliminating extraneous factors of $2$ in our discussion below; but working over $\mathbf{Z}$ also introduces new complications (see Remark 2.8) which we do not wish to address in the present article.

#### Construction 2.3.

The affine space $\mathbf{A}^{8}=\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}$ can be regarded as parametrizing cubes

$$ \textstyle{b_{2}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{d_{3}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{a\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{b_{1}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{d_{1}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{c,} \textstyle{b_{3}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{d_{2}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} $$

which we will represent by a tuple $(a,\vec{b},c,\vec{d})$ ; we will often use the symbol $\mathcal{C}$ to denote such a cube. If $\{e_{1},e_{2}\}$ are a basis for $\mathrm{std}$ , the above cube corresponds to the element of $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}$ given by

$$ \displaystyle ae_{1}\otimes e_{1}\otimes e_{1} \displaystyle+b_{1}e_{2}\otimes e_{1}\otimes e_{1}+b_{2}e_{1}\otimes e_{2}\otimes e_{1}+b_{3}e_{1}\otimes e_{1}\otimes e_{2} \displaystyle+d_{1}e_{1}\otimes e_{2}\otimes e_{2} \displaystyle+d_{2}e_{2}\otimes e_{1}\otimes e_{2}+d_{3}e_{2}\otimes e_{2}\otimes e_{1}+ce_{2}\otimes e_{2}\otimes e_{2}. $$

Associated to a cube $\mathcal{C}$ are three pairs of matrices, given by slicing along the top, leftmost, or front faces:

$$ \displaystyle M_{1}=\begin{pmatrix}a&b_{2}\\
b_{3}&d_{1}\end{pmatrix},\  \displaystyle N_{1}=\begin{pmatrix}b_{1}&d_{3}\\
d_{2}&c\end{pmatrix}, \displaystyle M_{2}=\begin{pmatrix}a&b_{1}\\
b_{3}&d_{2}\end{pmatrix},\  \displaystyle N_{2}=\begin{pmatrix}b_{2}&d_{3}\\
d_{1}&c\end{pmatrix}, \displaystyle M_{3}=\begin{pmatrix}a&b_{1}\\
b_{2}&d_{3}\end{pmatrix},\  \displaystyle N_{3}=\begin{pmatrix}b_{3}&d_{2}\\
d_{1}&c\end{pmatrix}; $$

each of these defines a binary quadratic form

$$ q_{i}(x,y)=-\mathrm{det}(M_{i}x+N_{i}y). $$

Explicitly,

$$ \displaystyle q_{1}(x,y) \displaystyle=\mathrm{det}(M_{1})x^{2}+(ac+b_{1}d_{1}-b_{2}d_{2}-b_{3}d_{3})xy+\mathrm{det}(N_{1})y^{2}, \displaystyle q_{2}(x,y) \displaystyle=\mathrm{det}(M_{2})x^{2}+(ac-b_{1}d_{1}+b_{2}d_{2}-b_{3}d_{3})xy+\mathrm{det}(N_{2})y^{2}, \displaystyle q_{3}(x,y) \displaystyle=\mathrm{det}(M_{3})x^{2}+(ac-b_{1}d_{1}-b_{2}d_{2}+b_{3}d_{3})xy+\mathrm{det}(N_{3})y^{2}. $$

Viewing $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast}$ as the space of binary quadratic forms as in Observation 2.1, these three quadratic forms define a map

$$ \mu:\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}\to\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast,\times 3}. $$

An easy check shows that this map is ${\check{{G}}}$ -equivariant.

#### Lemma 2.4 (Cayley, [Cay]).

The composite

$$ \mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}\xrightarrow{{\mu}}\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast,\times 3}\to\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast,\times 3}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}} $$

factors through the diagonal inclusion $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast}/\!\!/\mathrm{SL}_{2}\to\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast,\times 3}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}$ . In fact, the induced map $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}\to\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast}/\!\!/\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ defines an isomorphism

$$ \mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\xrightarrow{{\sim}}\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast}/\!\!/\mathrm{SL}_{2}\cong\mathbf{A}^{1}/\!\!/(\mathbf{Z}/2). $$

#### Proof.

The map $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast,\times 3}\to\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast,\times 3}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}$ sends a triple of matrices to their determinants, or equivalently a triple of quadratic forms to their discriminants. Therefore, we need to check that the three quadratic forms of Construction 2.3 have the same discriminant. This is easy: one finds that their common discriminant is

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{det}(q_{i}) \displaystyle=a^{2}c^{2}+b_{1}^{2}d_{1}^{2}+b_{2}^{2}d_{2}^{2}+b_{3}^{2}d_{3}^{2}-2(ab_{1}cd_{1}+ab_{2}cd_{2}+ab_{3}cd_{3} \displaystyle+b_{1}b_{2}d_{1}d_{2}+b_{1}b_{3}d_{1}d_{3}+b_{2}b_{3}d_{2}d_{3})+4(ad_{1}d_{2}d_{3}+b_{1}b_{2}b_{3}c). $$

It remains to show that the map $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\to\mathbf{A}^{1}$ defined by this polynomial is an isomorphism. This is stated/proved in [GKZ, Proposition 1.7 in Chapter 14], and is due to Cayley (see [Cay, Page 89] for the original source!). ∎

#### Notation 2.5.

Write $\mathrm{det}$ to denote the map $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}\to\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast}/\!\!/\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ from Lemma 2.4, so that if $\mathcal{C}$ is a cube, $\mathrm{det}(\mathcal{C})$ is the quantity of 1.

#### Remark 2.6.

The standard $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ -equivariant symplectic structure on $\mathrm{std}$ defines an $\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 3}$ -equivariant symplectic structure on $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}$ . This action is Hamiltonian, and one can verify by explicit calculation that the map $\mu:\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}\to\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast,\times 3}$ from Construction 2.3 is in fact simply the moment map for this $\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 3}$ -action. In other words, if $\omega_{1},\omega_{2},\omega_{3}$ denote the standard symplectic forms on the three copies of $\mathrm{std}$ , and $\omega=\omega_{1}\otimes\omega_{2}\otimes\omega_{3}$ is the resulting symplectic form on $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}$ , one can identify

$$ \mu:\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}\to\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast,\times 3},\ v\mapsto\left[\xi\mapsto\tfrac{1}{2}\omega(v,\xi v)\right]. $$

This gives a more “invariant” way to think about Bhargava’s three quadratic forms.

Along these lines, let us remark that [Bha1, Theorem 1] implies that the span

$$ \textstyle{\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\mu_{1}\times\mu_{2}} \scriptstyle{\mu_{3}} \textstyle{\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast}\times_{\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast}/\!\!/\mathrm{SL}_{2}}\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast}} \textstyle{\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast}} $$

given by the moment maps encodes Gauss composition on quadratic forms, in the sense that given two ( $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ -orbits of) quadratic forms $q_{1}$ and $q_{2}$ with the same discriminant, the ( $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ -orbit of) the Gauss composition $-(q_{1}+q_{2})$ is given by $\mu_{3}((\mu_{1}\times\mu_{2})^{-1}(q_{1},q_{2}))$ . The above span induces a span of stacks

$$ \textstyle{\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}/\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 3}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\mu_{1}\times\mu_{2}} \scriptstyle{\mu_{3}} \textstyle{(\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast}\times_{\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast}/\!\!/\mathrm{SL}_{2}}\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast})/(\mathrm{SL}_{2}\times\mathrm{SL}_{2})} \textstyle{\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast}/\mathrm{SL}_{2},} $$

which, using the isomorphism $\mathrm{Spin}_{4}\cong\mathrm{SL}_{2}\times\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ , can be identified with the Lagrangian correspondence [Dev, Corollary 3.6.20] for $H=\mathrm{SO}_{3}$ sitting inside $G=\mathrm{PSO}_{4}$ .

#### Remark 2.7.

An alternative way of constructing $\mathrm{det}(\mathcal{C})$ is as follows. Write $\mathcal{C}=e_{1}\otimes v_{1}+e_{2}\otimes v_{2}$ with $v_{1},v_{2}\in\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 2}\cong\mathbf{A}^{4}$ , and consider the symmetric bilinear form on $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 2}$ given by

$$ \langle{e_{1}\otimes e_{1},e_{2}\otimes e_{2}}\rangle=-\langle{e_{1}\otimes e_{2},e_{2}\otimes e_{1}}\rangle=1, $$

and all other pairings zero. This is the symmetric form on $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 2}$ induced from the standard symplectic form on $\mathrm{std}$ . Then, one can identify

$$ \mathrm{det}(\mathcal{C})=\mathrm{det}\begin{pmatrix}\langle{v_{1},v_{1}}\rangle&\langle{v_{1},v_{2}}\rangle\\
\langle{v_{2},v_{1}}\rangle&\langle{v_{2},v_{2}}\rangle\end{pmatrix}. $$

#### Remark 2.8.

Lemma 2.4 is not quite true over $\mathbf{F}_{2}$ (and hence not over $\mathbf{Z}$ ). One can already see the subtlety that arises over $\mathbf{F}_{2}$ from the formula 1: namely, the Cayley hyperdeterminant (appropriately normalized) admits a square root over $\mathbf{F}_{2}$ . Explicitly, if $\mathcal{C}=(a,\vec{b},c,\vec{d})$ is a cube and $\mathrm{det}(\mathcal{C})$ is defined by the formula 1, one has

$$ \frac{\mathrm{det}(\mathcal{C})}{2}\equiv\frac{(ac+b_{1}d_{1}+b_{2}d_{2}+b_{3}d_{3})^{2}}{2}\pmod{2}. $$

In fact, over an $\mathbf{F}_{2}$ -algebra, there is an analogue of Lemma 2.4 which states that the composite

$$ \mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}\to\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast,\times 3}\cong\mathfrak{pgl}_{2}^{\times 3}\xrightarrow{{\Tr}}(\mathbf{A}^{1})^{\times 3} $$

factors through the diagonal $\mathbf{A}^{1}\subseteq(\mathbf{A}^{1})^{\times 3}$ ; the resulting map $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}\to\mathbf{A}^{1}$ is given by the ${\check{{G}}}$ -invariant quadratic function

$$ \mathcal{C}\mapsto\Tr(\mathcal{C}):=ac+b_{1}d_{1}+b_{2}d_{2}+b_{3}d_{3}. $$

I expect that $\Tr$ defines an isomorphism $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\to\mathbf{A}^{1}$ over $\mathbf{F}_{2}$ , i.e., $\mathrm{H}^{0}({\check{{G}}};\Sym(\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3,\ast}))\cong\mathbf{F}_{2}[\Tr]$ . In particular, this means that the Cayley hyperdeterminant does not define an isomorphism $\mathrm{det}:\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\to\mathbf{A}^{1}$ over $\mathbf{F}_{2}$ .

However, I expect more to be true (this is based on discussions with Akshay Venkatesh). Namely, the moment map should induce an isomorphism of derived schemes

$$ \textstyle{\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}/\!\!/_{\mathrm{der}}{\check{{G}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\mu} \scriptstyle{\sim} \textstyle{\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast}/\!\!/_{\mathrm{der}}\mathrm{SL}_{2}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\mathrm{diag}} \textstyle{(\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast}/\!\!/_{\mathrm{der}}\mathrm{SL}_{2})^{\times 3}} $$

even over $\mathbf{Z}$ , where the symbol $/\!\!/_{\mathrm{der}}$ denotes the derived invariant-theoretic quotient (i.e., $V/\!\!/_{\mathrm{der}}H=\spec R\Gamma(BH;\Sym(V^{\ast}))$ ). We also expect that

$$ \mathrm{H}^{\ast}(\mathrm{SL}_{2,\mathbf{Z}};\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\Sym(\mathfrak{sl}_{2,\mathbf{Z}}(2)))\cong\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{\mathrm{SO}_{3}}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}). $$

There is an isomorphism $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{\mathrm{SO}_{3}}(\ast;\mathbf{Z})\cong\mathbf{Z}[p_{1},e]/2e$ , where the Euler class $e$ lives in cohomological degree $3$ . For example, the class $p_{1}$ should correspond to the determinant $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast}\to\mathbf{A}^{1}$ , and the fact that it has a square root modulo $2$ corresponds to the fact that the determinant map admits a square root over $\mathbf{F}_{2}$ , given by the trace $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast}\cong\mathfrak{pgl}_{2}\to\mathbf{A}^{1}$ . Similarly, the class $e$ should correspond to the nontrivial extension of $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast}\cong\Sym^{2}(\mathrm{std})$ given by $\mathfrak{gl}_{2}\cong\mathrm{std}\otimes\mathrm{std}$ .

We will now define an analogue of the Kostant slice, as it will be needed to apply [Dev, Theorem 3.6.4] (see [Dev, Strategy 1.2.1(b)]). For the purposes of our discussion, one should view this Kostant section as an analogue of the construction of the companion matrix associated to a characteristic polynomial.

#### Construction 2.9.

If $n$ is an integer, let $\vec{n}$ denote the triple $(n,n,n)$ . Let

$$ \kappa:\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast}/\!\!/\mathrm{SL}_{2}\cong\mathbf{A}^{1}/\!\!/(\mathbf{Z}/2)\cong\mathbf{A}^{1}\to\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3} $$

denote the map sending $a^{2}\mapsto(a^{2},\vec{0},0,\vec{1})$ . This corresponds to the cube

$$ \textstyle{0\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{1\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{a^{2}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{0\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{1\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{0.} \textstyle{0\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{1\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} $$

In this case, $\mathrm{det}(\kappa(a^{2}))=4a^{2}$ , so that $\kappa$ defines a section of $\mathrm{det}$ (at least up to the unit $4\in k^{\times}$ ). The associated quadratic forms are all equal, and are given by

$$ q_{1}(x,y)=q_{2}(x,y)=q_{3}(x,y)=a^{2}x^{2}-y^{2}, $$

which corresponds to the traceless matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ a^{2}&0\end{pmatrix}\in\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast}$ . (Note that this is exactly the companion matrix associated to the characteristic polynomial $y^{2}-a^{2}$ .)

#### Remark 2.10.

Fix an integer $n$ . Then the ${\check{{G}}}$ -variety $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}$ admits a natural grading, where the entries of a cube $(a,\vec{b},c,\vec{d})$ have the following weights: $a$ lives in weight $-4n$ , $b$ lives in weight $-2n$ , $c$ lives in weight $2n$ , and $d$ lives in weight $0$ . Write $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}(4n,\vec{2n},-2n,\vec{0})$ to denote the associated graded variety. Equip $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast}$ with the grading where the entries of a matrix $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&-a\end{pmatrix}$ have the following weights: $a$ lives in weight $-2n$ , $b$ lives in weight $0$ , and $c$ lives in weight $-4n$ . Similarly, equip $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ with the grading coming from $2n\rho$ , so that the entries of a matrix $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}$ have the following weights: $a$ and $d$ live in weight $0$ , $b$ lives in weight $2n$ , and $c$ lives in weight $-2n$ . With these gradings, the $\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 3}$ -equivariant map $\mu:\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}\to\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast,\times 3}$ is a graded map, and $\kappa$ defines a graded map $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast}(2n)/\!\!/\mathrm{SL}_{2}\cong\mathbf{A}^{1}(4n)\to\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}(4n,\vec{2n},-2n,\vec{0})$ . The cases $n=1$ and $n=3$ will be relevant below (corresponding to Theorem 1.2 and Theorem 1.5, respectively).

#### Remark 2.11.

As mentioned in Remark 1.9, the quotient stack $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}/\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 3}$ is studied in quantum information theory. For instance, in [DVC], Dür-Vidal-Cirac study the orbit structure of $\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 3}$ acting on $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}$ (in particular, they recover Figure 1 independently of [GKZ]). See also [CKW], where the Cayley hyperdeterminant is rediscovered as [CKW, Equations 20 and 21].

For the interested reader, let us describe the translation between our notation/terminology and that of quantum information theory. Our base field will now be $\mathbf{C}$ . An element of $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes n}$ (really, of the projective space $\mathbf{P}(\mathrm{std}^{\otimes n})\cong\mathbf{P}^{2^{n}-1}$ ) is called an $n$ -qubit, and the action of $\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times n}$ is via stochastic local operations and classical communication (SLOCC) operators (replacing $\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times n}$ by $\mathrm{GL}_{2}^{\times n}$ simply amounts to dropping the word “stochastic”). The space $\mathrm{std}$ is equipped with a basis $\{|0\rangle,|1\rangle\}$ , and a cube $\mathcal{C}=(a,\vec{b},c,\vec{d})\in\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}$ corresponds to the three-qubit66 6 Technically, a qubit is required to have norm $1$ , so one must rescale $\mathcal{C}$ by $\sqrt{a^{2}+\|\vec{b}\|^{2}+c^{2}+\|\vec{d}\|^{2}}$ ; but this could in theory introduce a singularity when $a^{2}+\|\vec{b}\|^{2}+c^{2}+\|\vec{d}\|^{2}=0$ . We will ignore this (important!) point below.

$$ \displaystyle a|000\rangle \displaystyle+b_{1}|100\rangle+b_{2}|010\rangle+b_{3}|001\rangle \displaystyle+d_{1}|011\rangle \displaystyle+d_{2}|101\rangle+d_{3}|110\rangle+c|111\rangle. $$

Here, the bra-ket notation $|ijk\rangle$ means $|i\rangle\otimes|j\rangle\otimes|k\rangle$ . The state

$$ \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1,\vec{0},1,\vec{0})=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(|000\rangle+|111\rangle\right) $$

is known as the Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger (GHZ) state, and the state

$$ \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\kappa(0)=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(0,\vec{1},0,\vec{0})=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\left(|001\rangle+|010\rangle+|100\rangle\right) $$

is called the W state. These two states are known to represent two very different kinds of quantum entanglement; the reason for this is simply that the Cayley hyperdeterminant of the GHZ state is nonzero, but the Cayley hyperdeterminant of the W state vanishes. Nevertheless, the proof of Proposition 2.15 shows that there is a natural degeneration of (the SLOCC/ $\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 3}$ -equivalence class of) the GHZ state into the W state. (This degeneration is $\kappa(a^{2})$ , whose norm is $\sqrt{a^{4}+3}$ ; in particular, it passes through zero when $a=\sqrt[4]{-3}$ , and so this one-parameter family is not physical!) In fact, this state already appears as [DVC, Equation 20].

One of the key properties of the Kostant section/companion matrices is that a matrix $A\in\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\ast}$ is conjugate to $\kappa(\mathrm{det}(A))$ if and only if $A$ is regular (i.e., the minimal polynomial of $A$ agrees with its characteristic polynomial), if and only if $A$ is nonzero. We will now prove an analogous result concerning $\kappa:\mathbf{A}^{1}\to\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}$ .

#### Proposition 2.12.

The ${\check{{G}}}$ -orbit of the image of $\kappa$ is a dense open subscheme whose complement has codimension $3$ .

#### Proof.

We will use the classification of ${\check{{G}}}$ -orbits on $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}$ as in [GKZ, Example 4.5 in Chapter 14]; see Figure 1 for a graph of the seven orbits of ${\check{{G}}}$ on $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}$ . Namely, if $\lambda\neq 0$ , all elements of $\mathrm{det}^{-1}(\lambda)$ are in a single ${\check{{G}}}$ -orbit. (In fact, all elements in the fiber $\mathrm{det}^{-1}(1)$ are in the ${\check{{G}}}$ -orbit of $(1,\vec{0},1,\vec{0})$ .) The ${\check{{G}}}$ -orbit of $\mathrm{det}^{-1}(\mathbf{G}_{m})$ is open and dense, and hence is $8$ -dimensional; moreover, it agrees with the ${\check{{G}}}$ -orbit of $\kappa(\mathbf{G}_{m})$ . Next, there is a maximal ${\check{{G}}}$ -orbit inside the fiber $\mathrm{det}^{-1}(0)$ , given by the orbit of $(0,\vec{0},0,\vec{1})=\kappa(0)$ . This orbit is $7$ -dimensional, and the largest ${\check{{G}}}$ -orbits contained in the complement $\mathrm{det}^{-1}(0)-{\check{{G}}}\cdot\kappa(0)$ have dimension $5$ . In particular, the complement of ${\check{{G}}}\cdot\kappa(\mathbf{A}^{1})\subseteq\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3}$ has dimension $5$ , i.e., codimension $8-5=3$ . ∎

As explained in [GKZ, Example 4.5 in Chapter 14], the closure of the associated orbits inside $\mathbf{P}(\mathrm{std}^{\otimes 3})=\mathbf{P}^{7}$ can be described as follows. #### Remark 2.14.

More generally, let $\mathrm{std}_{n}$ denote the standard $n$ -dimensional representation of $\mathrm{SO}_{n}$ , so that the symplectic vector space $\mathrm{std}\otimes\mathrm{std}_{n}$ is equipped with an action of $\mathrm{SL}_{2}\times\mathrm{SO}_{n}$ . $$ (\mathrm{std}\otimes\mathrm{std}_{n})/\!\!/(\mathrm{SL}_{2}\times\mathrm{SO}_{n})\cong\mathbf{A}^{1}/\!\!/(\mathbf{Z}/2). $$

If we allow ourselves a square root of $2$ , then Proposition 2.12 admits an analogue in this more general setting (at least if one works over $\mathbf{C}$ ): there is a Kostant slice $\kappa:\mathbf{A}^{1}/\!\!/(\mathbf{Z}/2)\to\mathrm{std}\otimes\mathrm{std}_{n}$ whose $\mathrm{SL}_{2}\times\mathrm{SO}_{n}$ -orbit is open and has complement of codimension $3$ . Namely, assume $n=2j$ is even for simplicity (a slight variant of this construction will work for odd $n$ ), so that without loss of generality, the symmetric bilinear form on $\mathrm{std}_{n}$ is given by $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix}^{\oplus j}$ . If $e_{1},\cdots,e_{2j}$ is a basis for $\mathrm{std}_{n}$ , let $v_{1}=a^{2}e_{1}+e_{2}$ , and let $v_{2}=\sum_{i=2}^{j}(e_{2i-1}+e_{2i})$ . Then $\langle{v_{1},v_{1}}\rangle=2a^{2}$ , $\langle{v_{2},v_{2}}\rangle=2(j-1)$ , and $\langle{v_{1},v_{2}}\rangle=0$ . If $e_{1},e_{2}$ is a basis for $\mathrm{std}$ , the Kostant slice sends

$$ \kappa:\mathbf{A}^{1}/\!\!/(\mathbf{Z}/2)\to\mathrm{std}\otimes\mathrm{std}_{n},\ a^{2}\mapsto\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}e_{1}\otimes v_{1}+\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2(j-1)}}e_{2}\otimes v_{2}. $$

It is easy to check that this map does indeed give a section of $\mathrm{det}$ . To check that the $\mathrm{SL}_{2}\times\mathrm{SO}_{n}$ -orbit of $\kappa$ has complement of codimension $3$ , we need an analogue of Remark 2.13. This succumbs to an analysis similar to that of [GKZ, Chapter 14]. One finds that if $n\geq 5$ , the poset of closures of $\mathrm{SL}_{2}\times\mathrm{SO}_{n}$ -orbits in $\mathbf{P}(\mathrm{std}\otimes\mathrm{std}_{n})\cong\mathbf{P}^{2n-1}$ is as shown in Figure 2. The case $n=4$ is “degenerate” and one instead gets Figure 1.
