$$ \mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{P_{\lambda}}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})\cong\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})[x,c^{\prime}_{n-1}]/(xc^{\prime}_{n-1}=c_{n},\ x^{2n-2}-p_{1}x^{2n-4}-\cdots-p_{n-1}+{c^{\prime}_{n-1}}^{2}). $$

As an $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ -module, this is indeed isomorphic to $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})\otimes\mathrm{std}_{2n}$ . Building on Example 6.11 shows that as a group scheme over $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ , the functor of points of ${\check{{J}}}$ sends an $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ -algebra $R$ to the subgroup of those units $f(x,c^{\prime}_{n-1})\in(\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{P_{\lambda}}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})\otimes_{\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})}R)^{\times}$ such that $f(x,c^{\prime}_{n-1})^{-1}=f(-x,-c^{\prime}_{n-1})$ . The action of ${\check{{J}}}$ on $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{P_{\lambda}}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ preserves the symmetric bilinear form given by

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{P_{\lambda}}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})\otimes_{\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})}\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{P_{\lambda}}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}) \displaystyle\xrightarrow{\langle{-,-}\rangle}\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}) \displaystyle f,g \displaystyle\mapsto\text{coefficient of }x^{2n-2}\text{ in }f(x,c^{\prime}_{n-1})g(-x,-c^{\prime}_{n-1}). $$

Geometrically, this bilinear form comes from $G$ -equivariant Poincaré duality on $G/P_{\lambda}$ , twisted by the natural action of $\mathbf{Z}/2$ on $G/P_{\lambda}$ . (This $\mathbf{Z}/2$ acts on $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{P_{\lambda}}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ by sending $x\mapsto-x$ and $c^{\prime}_{n-1}\mapsto-c^{\prime}_{n-1}$ .) The bilinear form $\langle{-,-}\rangle$ on $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{P_{\lambda}}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ gives the desired factorization 6.8 of the map ${{\check{{J}}}}\to\mathrm{GL}_{2n}\times\mathfrak{t}/\!\!/W$ through the inclusion $\mathrm{SO}_{2n}\times\mathfrak{t}/\!\!/W\hookrightarrow\mathrm{GL}_{2n}\times\mathfrak{t}/\!\!/W$ .

As we have seen, the calculation of Theorem 6.3 is quite powerful. Here is another simple application, motivated by [GK] and [GR3]; see also [Dev3, Example 3.6.13], where the same example is presented.

#### Proposition 6.15 (Gelfand-Graev action).

The natural action of ${\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{T}}}$ on the affine closure $\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}$ extends to an action of ${\check{{G}}}\times(W\rtimes{\check{{T}}})$ , where $W$ is the Weyl group.

#### Proof.

Let $T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})_{\mathrm{reg}}={\check{{G}}}\times^{{\check{{N}}}}{\check{{\mathfrak{n}}}}^{\perp}_{\mathrm{reg}}$ denote the regular locus in $T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})$ ; then $T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})_{\mathrm{reg}}\subseteq T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})$ is open, with complement of codimension $2$ , so that $\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}\cong\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})_{\mathrm{reg}}}$ . Note that there is an isomorphism

$$ {\check{{G}}}\backslash T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})_{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{T}}}\cong{\check{{\mathfrak{n}}}}^{\perp}_{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{B}}}, $$

so (the proof of) Corollary 6.8 gives isomorphisms

$$ T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})_{\mathrm{reg}}\cong({\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{T}}})\times^{{\check{{B}}}}{\check{{\mathfrak{n}}}}^{\perp}_{\mathrm{reg}}\cong({\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{T}}}\times(\psi+{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}))/\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}. $$

There is a canonical $W$ -action on ${\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{T}}}\times(\psi+{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast})$ , given by the natural $W$ -actions on ${\check{{T}}}$ and on $\psi+{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}\cong{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}$ . Similarly, $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}$ also admits a natural $W$ -action; it is given via Theorem 6.3 by the natural $W$ -action on $\mathrm{H}^{T_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ . Moreover, the closed immersion

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}\to{\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{T}}}\times(\psi+{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}) $$

is $W$ -equivariant (indeed, the map $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}\to{\check{{T}}}\times(\psi+{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast})$ is induced by the inclusion $\mathrm{H}^{T_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{T};\mathbf{Q})\to\mathrm{H}^{T_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ on equivariant homology). This implies that the quotient of 6.9 admits a $W$ -action, which defines a $W$ -action on the affine closure of $T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})_{\mathrm{reg}}$ as desired. ∎

Note that we assumed in Corollary 6.8 that $G$ is simply-laced; but this is not necessary, because we know (by the discussion in Section 2) that the main result of [ABG] implies Corollary 6.8 is true for any connected reductive $G$ . Alternatively, one can observe that the proof of Corollary 6.8 itself never seriously appeals to $G$ being simply-laced.

#### Remark 6.16.

The proof of Proposition 6.15 generalizes to show that if ${\check{{P}}}\subseteq{\check{{G}}}$ is a parabolic subgroup with Levi quotient ${\check{{L}}}$ and unipotent radical $U_{{\check{{P}}}}$ , then the natural action of ${\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{L}}}$ on the affine closure $\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/U_{{\check{{P}}}})}$ extends to an action of ${\check{{G}}}\times(W_{L}\rtimes{\check{{L}}})$ , where $W_{L}=N_{{\check{{G}}}}({\check{{L}}})/{\check{{L}}}$ is the Weyl group. (Also see [Gan3].)

The $W$ -action of Proposition 6.15 is known as the (semiclassical) Gelfand-Graev action. The moment map $\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}$ is $W$ -equivariant for the trivial action on the target. There is a commutative diagram

$$ \textstyle{\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}} $$

which relates $\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}$ to the Grothendieck-Springer resolution; and via this diagram, the Gelfand-Graev action is closely related to the Weyl action in Springer theory.

#### Example 6.17.

When ${\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ , the affine closure $\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}$ is simply $T^{\ast}(\mathbf{A}^{2})$ , and the $W=\mathbf{Z}/2$ -action on it is given by the symplectic Fourier transform. To see this, let ${\check{{J}}}_{X}$ denote the kernel of the homomorphism $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}\to{\check{{T}}}\times(\psi+{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast})$ of group schemes over $\psi+{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}$ . (This follows the notation from [Dev3].) Then 6.9 gives an isomorphism

$$ ({\check{{G}}}\times(\psi+{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}))/{\check{{J}}}_{X}\xrightarrow{\cong}T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})_{\mathrm{reg}}. $$

In the case at hand, $\psi+{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}\cong\mathbf{A}^{1}$ with coordinate $x$ , and the group scheme ${\check{{J}}}_{X}$ is just $\spec\mathbf{Z}[x,b]/bx$ (where the group law sends $b\mapsto b\otimes 1+1\otimes b$ ). The above isomorphism defines a map

$$ q:\mathrm{SL}_{2}\times\mathbf{A}^{1}\to\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}=T^{\ast}(\mathbf{A}^{2}), $$

and the affine closure of the image is all of $T^{\ast}(\mathbf{A}^{2})$ . The map $q$ can be explicitly described as follows. View a point of $T^{\ast}(\mathbf{A}^{2})$ as a pair $\left(\begin{pmatrix}u_{1}\\ u_{2}\end{pmatrix},(v_{1},v_{2})\right)$ of a vector and a covector. Then $q$ is the natural extension to $\mathrm{SL}_{2}\times\mathbf{A}^{1}$ of the map $\kappa:\mathbf{A}^{1}\to T^{\ast}(\mathbf{A}^{2})$ which sends $x\mapsto\left(\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 0\end{pmatrix},(x,0)\right)$ . In other words, $q$ sends

$$ (g,x)=\left(\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\
c&d\end{pmatrix},x\right)\mapsto\left(g\begin{pmatrix}1\\
0\end{pmatrix},(g^{T})^{-1}(x,0)\right)=\left(\begin{pmatrix}a\\
c\end{pmatrix},(dx,-bx)\right). $$

Of course, one could also swap the roles of $\mathbf{A}^{2}$ and $(\mathbf{A}^{2})^{\ast}$ in $T^{\ast}(\mathbf{A}^{2})$ ; the map $\kappa$ would then send $x\mapsto\left(\begin{pmatrix}0\\ x\end{pmatrix},(0,1)\right)$ , and $q$ would send

$$ (g,x)=\left(\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\
c&d\end{pmatrix},x\right)\mapsto\left(\begin{pmatrix}0\\
x\end{pmatrix}\cdot g^{T},(0,1)\cdot g^{-1}\right)=\left(\begin{pmatrix}bx\\
dx\end{pmatrix},(-c,a)\right). $$

If we compose with the involution sending $x\mapsto-x$ , the resulting involution

$$ \left(\begin{pmatrix}a\\
c\end{pmatrix},(dx,-bx)\right)\mapsto\left(\begin{pmatrix}-bx\\
-dx\end{pmatrix},(-c,a)\right). $$

This, of course, is precisely the symplectic Fourier transform, which sends

$$ \left(\begin{pmatrix}u_{1}\\
u_{2}\end{pmatrix},(v_{1},v_{2})\right)\mapsto\left(\begin{pmatrix}v_{2}\\
-v_{1}\end{pmatrix},(-u_{2},u_{1})\right). $$

We also have the following, which is an obvious consequence of Corollary 2.7 and Corollary 2.11 (but can be reproved using Corollary 6.8).

#### Proposition 6.18.

Let $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\heartsuit}$ denote the heart of the $t$ -structure on $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)=\mathrm{coMod}_{\pi_{0}(\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G}))^{\vee}}(\QCoh(\mathfrak{t}))$ coming from the standard (homological truncation) $t$ -structure on $\QCoh(\mathfrak{t})$ . Then, the composite functor

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\simeq\QCoh(\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}})\to\QCoh({\check{{G}}}\backslash\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}}) $$

is $t$ -exact, and on hearts, it restricts to a fully faithful functor on the essential image of the functor 6.4. Furthermore, this functor is $W$ -equivariant for the natural action of $W=\mathrm{N}_{G_{c}}(T_{c})/T_{c}$ on the left-hand side and the Gelfand-Graev action of Proposition 6.15 on the right-hand side.

Similarly, let $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\heartsuit}$ denote the heart of the $t$ -structure on $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)=\mathrm{coMod}_{\pi_{0}(\mathcal{F}_{G}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G}))^{\vee}}(\QCoh(\mathfrak{t}/\!\!/W))$ coming from the standard (homological truncation) $t$ -structure on $\QCoh(\mathfrak{t}/\!\!/W)$ . Then, the composite functor

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)\simeq\QCoh({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast,\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}})\to\QCoh({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/{\check{{G}}}) $$

is $t$ -exact, and on hearts, it restricts to a fully faithful functor on the essential image of the functor $\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})\to\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ (analogous to 6.3).

#### Proof.

If $V\in\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})$ , the object $\mathcal{S}_{k}(V)$ lies in $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\heartsuit}$ , and we need to show that there is an isomorphism

$$ \mathrm{Map}_{\QCoh({\check{{G}}}\backslash\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}})^{\heartsuit}}(V_{1}\otimes_{\mathbf{Q}}\mathcal{O}_{\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}},V_{2}\otimes_{\mathbf{Q}}\mathcal{O}_{\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}})\\
\xrightarrow{\cong}\mathrm{Map}_{\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\heartsuit}}(\mathcal{S}_{k}(V_{1}),\mathcal{S}_{k}(W_{1})) $$

of $\mathbf{Q}$ -vector spaces for any two representations $V_{1},V_{2}\in\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})$ . In other words, By Corollary 6.8, there is an isomorphism

$$ \mathrm{Map}_{\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\heartsuit}}(\mathcal{S}_{k}(V),\mathcal{S}_{k}(W))\cong\mathrm{Map}_{\QCoh(\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}})^{\heartsuit}}(V\otimes_{\mathbf{Q}}\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}},W\otimes_{\mathbf{Q}}\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}}). $$

Since $\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}}\hookrightarrow{\check{{G}}}\backslash\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}}$ has complement of codimension $2$ and $\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}$ is affine and normal, the algebraic Hartogs lemma implies that the restriction map

$$ \mathrm{Map}_{\QCoh({\check{{G}}}\backslash\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}})^{\heartsuit}}(V\otimes_{\mathbf{Q}}\mathcal{O}_{\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}},W\otimes_{\mathbf{Q}}\mathcal{O}_{\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}})\\
\to\mathrm{Map}_{\QCoh(\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}})^{\heartsuit}}(V\otimes_{\mathbf{Q}}\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}},W\otimes_{\mathbf{Q}}\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}}) $$

is an isomorphism, as desired. (This is where it is crucial that we work at the level of abelian categories.) The same argument works for $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ ; in this case, ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast,\mathrm{reg}}\hookrightarrow{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}$ even has complement of codimension $3$ . ∎

Proposition 6.18 gives an analogue of [BF, Theorem 4]: namely, if $\QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/{\check{{G}}})$ denotes the essential image of the pullback functor $\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})\to\QCoh({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/{\check{{G}}})$ , then there is a fully faithful embedding

$$ \QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/{\check{{G}}})^{\heartsuit}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\heartsuit}. $$

Similarly, if $\QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}({\check{{G}}}\backslash\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}})$ denotes the essential image of the pullback functor $\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{T}}})\to\QCoh({\check{{G}}}\backslash\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}})$ , then there is a fully faithful embedding

$$ \QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}({\check{{G}}}\backslash\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}})^{\heartsuit}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\heartsuit}. $$

Let $\mathrm{Rep}_{\mathrm{min}}({\check{{G}}})$ denote the idempotent completion of the subcategory of $\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})$ spanned by tensor products of irreducible ${\check{{G}}}$ -representations with minuscule highest weights. In general, if ${\check{{G}}}$ is simple (but not necessarily simply-laced) and not of types $G_{2}$ , $F_{4}$ , or $E_{8}$ , then any representation is a summand of a tensor product of irreducible ${\check{{G}}}$ -representations with minuscule highest weights, so that $\mathrm{Rep}_{\mathrm{min}}({\check{{G}}})\simeq\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})$ .1717 17 When ${\check{{G}}}$ is of types $G_{2}$ , $F_{4}$ , or $E_{8}$ , there are no minuscule weights at all. In general, $\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})$ is the idempotent completion of its full subcategory spanned by tensor products of irreducible ${\check{{G}}}$ -representations with minuscule and quasi-minuscule highest weights.

#### Corollary 6.19.

Let $\QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/{\check{{G}}})^{\mathrm{min},\heartsuit}$ denote the essential image of $\mathrm{Rep}_{\mathrm{min}}({\check{{G}}})$ under the pullback functor $\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})^{\heartsuit}\to\QCoh({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/{\check{{G}}})^{\heartsuit}$ (so it is the entirety of $\QCoh({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/{\check{{G}}})^{\heartsuit}$ if ${\check{{G}}}$ is not of type $E_{8}$ ). Similarly, let $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\mathrm{min},\heartsuit}$ denote the idempotent completion of the subcategory of $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\heartsuit}$ spanned by $\mathcal{F}_{\lambda_{\bullet}}^{\mathrm{gr}}$ ranging over sequences $\lambda_{\bullet}$ of minuscule highest weights. Then there is an equivalence

$$ \QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/{\check{{G}}})^{\mathrm{min},\heartsuit}\simeq\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\mathrm{min},\heartsuit}. $$

There is a similar equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\mathrm{min},\heartsuit}\simeq\QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}({\check{{G}}}\backslash\overline{T^{\ast}({\check{{G}}}/{\check{{N}}})}/{\check{{T}}})^{\mathrm{min},\heartsuit}, $$

where these categories are defined analogously by idempotent completion.

Note that the category $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\mathrm{min},\heartsuit}$ is the heart of a degeneration, in the sense of Section 4, of the similarly-defined category $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\mathrm{min}}$ . (In particular, Corollary 6.19 gives an equivalence between the purely algebraically defined category $\QCoh_{\mathrm{free}}({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/{\check{{G}}})^{\mathrm{min},\heartsuit}$ and a degeneration of the purely topologically defined category $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\mathrm{min}}$ .) If $\lambda_{\bullet}$ and $\mu_{\bullet}$ are two sequences of dominant minuscule weights of ${\check{{G}}}$ , there is an equivalence of $k$ -modules

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{Map}_{\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\mathrm{min}}}(\mathcal{F}_{\lambda_{\bullet}},\mathcal{F}_{\mu_{\bullet}}) \displaystyle\simeq\mathcal{F}_{G}(\overline{\mathrm{Gr}_{G}^{\lambda_{\bullet}}})\otimes_{\mathrm{coMod}_{\mathcal{F}_{G}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}}(\QCoh(\mathcal{M}_{G}))}\mathcal{F}_{G}(\overline{\mathrm{Gr}_{G}^{\mu_{\bullet}}}) \displaystyle\simeq\mathcal{F}_{G}(\overline{\mathrm{Gr}_{G}^{\lambda_{\bullet}}}\times_{\mathrm{Gr}_{G}}\overline{\mathrm{Gr}_{G}^{\mu_{\bullet}}}), $$

where the final equivalence uses the Künneth formula at the level of $k$ -cochains. The category $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)^{\mathrm{min}}$ therefore compares to (the $k$ -analogue of) the category from [CK, Section 3.4].

At first glance, the existence of the $t$ -structure on $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ from Proposition 6.18 may perhaps be a bit surprising, since $k$ is a $2$ -periodic ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring. In fact, this periodicity prohibits $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ itself from having a $t$ -structure. However, the $\infty$ -category $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ “flattens” out the homological periodicity in $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ to a weight periodicity, but it is itself also a stable $\infty$ -category. In particular, it has a homological shift operation, which is distinct from the operation of shifting weights (just as with the usual category of mixed sheaves). (The $2$ -periodicity of $k$ implies that the weight-shifting operation on $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ is an equivalence, which is why we do not see gradings/weights when discussing $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ ; but the weight-shifting operation will be nontrivial on, say, $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ .) The resulting homological shift on $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};k)$ is no longer periodic, and it is therefore reasonable to equip this $\infty$ -category with a $t$ -structure. (This $t$ -structure is unrelated to the perverse $t$ -structure on $\mathrm{Shv}_{I}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ .)

We will now discuss a deformation quantization of Corollary 6.8 by adding loop-rotation equivariance. Write $\widetilde{T}=T\times\mathbf{G}_{m}^{\mathrm{rot}}$ to denote the corresponding affine torus. In the case when $G$ is a torus, we have already discussed this in Section 5. For more general $G$ , this turns out to be a bit tricky: while $\mathrm{H}^{T_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ is a bicommutative Hopf algebra1818 18 To be more precise, the ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -space structure on $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ equips $C^{T_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ with the structure of an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -algebra in ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -coalgebras over $C_{T_{c}}^{\ast}(\ast;\mathbf{Q})$ ., the loop-rotation equivariant homology $\mathrm{H}^{\widetilde{T}_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ is only a cocommutative coalgebroid over $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{\widetilde{T}_{c}}(\ast;\mathbf{Q})$ . That is, it does not admit an algebra structure. While this is not a mathematical issue, it does make the task of explicitly understanding $\mathrm{H}^{\widetilde{T}_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ in a satisfactory way more complicated. Instead, it turns out to be easier to describe $\mathrm{H}^{\widetilde{T}_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Fl}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ , where $\mathrm{Fl}_{G}$ is the affine flag variety, defined as the quotient $G(\!(t)\!)/I$ for the Iwahori subgroup $I\subseteq G[\![t]\!]$ associated to a Borel subgroup $B\subseteq G$ . To state the result, we need a definition from [GKV2].

#### Definition 6.20.

Let $(\Lambda,\Phi,{\check{{\Lambda}}},{\check{{\Phi}}})$ be a root datum with associated Weyl group $W$ and torus $T=\Hom(\Lambda,\mathbf{G}_{m})$ . Let $\Delta$ be a base of simple roots, let $\Phi^{+}$ denote the corresponding set of positive roots, and let $\Phi^{\prime}$ denote the subset $W\cdot\Delta\subseteq\Phi$ . Let $\mathbf{H}$ be a $1$ -dimensional group scheme (over a commutative ring $R$ ). As in Definition 5.1, let $\mathbf{H}_{T}=\Hom(\Lambda,T)$ , and for each character $\lambda\in\Lambda$ , let $\mathbf{H}_{T_{\lambda}}\hookrightarrow\mathbf{H}_{T}$ denote the subgroup corresponding to the subtorus $T_{\lambda}=\ker(\lambda)\subseteq T$ . Let $Q(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}})$ denote the sheaf of functions on the generic point of $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}}$ . The twisted group algebra $Q(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}})[W]$ is the algebra which is additively given by the tensor product $Q(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}})\otimes_{F}F[W]$ , and whose multiplication law is given by

$$ (f_{1}\otimes w_{1})\cdot(f_{2}\otimes w_{2})=(f\cdot w_{1}g)\otimes(w_{1}w_{2}). $$

The algebra $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{H},T,W)$ is defined to be the subset of $Q(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}})[W]$ of those elements $\sum_{w\in W}f_{w}[w]$ such that:

- • The poles of $f_{x}$ all have order $\leq 1$ , and these are contained in the divisors $\mathbf{H}_{T_{\alpha}}$ for each $\alpha\in\Phi^{\prime}$ .

- • For each $w\in W$ and $\alpha\in\Phi^{+}\cap\Phi^{\prime}$ , we have

$$ \mathrm{Res}_{\mathbf{H}_{T_{\alpha}}}(f_{w})+\mathrm{Res}_{\mathbf{H}_{T_{\alpha}}}(f_{s_{\alpha}w})=0. $$

In [GKV2], this algebra is denoted $\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}$ . It is proved in [GKV2, Theorem 1.4] that $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{H},T,W)$ is a subalgebra of $Q(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}})[W]$ .

#### Remark 6.21.

The pair $(Q(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}}),Q(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}})[W])$ admits the structure of a (cocommutative) Hopf algebroid; we will abusively say that $Q(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}})[W]$ admits the structure of a Hopf $Q(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}})$ -algebroid. The coproduct comes from the diagonal on $W$ ; the left unit comes from the inclusion $Q(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}})\subseteq Q(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}})[W]$ ; and the right unit comes from the action of $W$ on $\mathbf{H}_{T}$ (which defines a coaction of $W$ on $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}}$ that extends to a coaction on $Q(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}})$ ). The resulting Hopf $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}}$ -algebroid structure on $Q(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}})[W]$ restricts to $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{H},T,W)$ , so that $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{H},T,W)$ admits the structure of a (cocommutative) Hopf $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}}$ -algebroid. (See [Woj, Theorem 4.11] for the case $\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{G}_{a}$ .)

When $W$ is finite, [GKV2, Proposition 2.3] states that upon rationalization, the action of $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{H},T,W)$ on $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}}$ gives an isomorphism between $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{H},T,W)$ and $\End_{\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}}^{W}}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}})$ . This gives a Morita equivalence between the category of $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{H},T,W)$ -modules and the category of $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}}^{W}$ -modules. Under this equivalence, the symmetric monoidal structure on the category of $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{H},T,W)$ -modules from the cocommutative Hopf algebroid structure on $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{H},T,W)$ identifies with the standard symmetric monoidal structure on the category of $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{T}}^{W}$ -modules.

If $\Lambda$ denotes the coroot lattice of ${G}$ , let $W^{\mathrm{aff}}=\Lambda\rtimes W$ denote the corresponding affine Weyl group, and let $\widetilde{W}=\mathbb{X}_{\ast}({T})\rtimes W$ denote the extended affine Weyl group.1919 19 The affine Weyl group $W^{\mathrm{aff}}$ introduced above is very slightly different from the affine Weyl group studied in [Gin, Section 7.2] or [Gan2]; the affine Weyl group there is the semidirect product $W^{\prime\mathrm{aff}}={\check{{\Lambda}}}\rtimes W$ , where ${\check{{\Lambda}}}$ is the root lattice of $G$ . When $G$ is simply-laced, these are, of course, isomorphic; but they differ otherwise. For clarity, note that the action of $\widetilde{W}$ on $\mathbb{X}^{\ast}(T)$ (and hence on $\mathbf{H}_{T}$ ) is given as follows: if $\alpha$ is a coweight of $T$ and $n\in\mathbf{Z}$ , the generator $s_{\alpha,n}$ of $W^{\mathrm{aff}}$ acts on $\mathbb{X}^{\ast}(T)$ by reflection along the affine hyperplane $\{x\in\mathbb{X}^{\ast}(T)|\langle{x,\alpha}\rangle=n\}$ . #### Theorem 6.24.

There is an isomorphism of associative $\mathbf{Q}[\hbar]$ -algebras

$$ \mathrm{H}^{\widetilde{T}_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Fl}_{G};\mathbf{Q})\cong\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{G}_{a},\widetilde{T},\widetilde{W}). $$

Here, $\mathrm{H}^{\widetilde{T}_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Fl}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ is equipped with the associative algebra structure coming from convolution. #### Proof.

The affine flag variety $\mathrm{Fl}_{G}$ is an ind-finite GKM space in the sense of Definition 3.12, and so we may use Proposition 3.15 to describe $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}^{\widetilde{T}_{c}}(\mathrm{Fl}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ . The GKM graph of $\mathrm{Fl}_{G}$ has set of vertices given by $\mathrm{Fl}_{G}^{\widetilde{T}_{c}}=\mathbb{X}_{\ast}(T)\rtimes W\cong\widetilde{W}$ , and an edge $w\to s_{\alpha,n}w$ for each affine reflection $s_{\alpha,n}\in\widetilde{W}$ . In particular, if ${\overset{\circ}{\widetilde{\mathfrak{t}}}}$ denotes the complement of the union of affine hyperplanes in $\widetilde{\mathfrak{t}}$ , then $\mathrm{H}^{\widetilde{T}_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Fl}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ is a subalgebra of $\mathrm{H}^{\widetilde{T}_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Fl}_{G}^{\widetilde{T}_{c}};\mathbf{Q})|_{{\overset{\circ}{\widetilde{\mathfrak{t}}}}}$ . $$ \mathrm{H}^{\widetilde{T}_{c}}_{\ast}(\mathrm{Fl}_{G};\mathbf{Q})\subseteq Q(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{H}_{\widetilde{T}}})[\widetilde{W}]\supseteq\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{G}_{a},\widetilde{T},\widetilde{W}). $$

## 7. The K-theoretic story

Our goal in this section is to prove an analogue of Corollary 6.8, albeit with coefficients in $k=\mathrm{KU}$ . Note that in this case, $\mathcal{M}_{T,0}\cong T$ . To do so, we need an analogue of Definition 6.1 and constructions surrounding it. Recall that the group $G$ (over $\mathbf{C}$ ) is connected, almost simple, and simply-laced. We will also fix an algebraically closed field $F$ ,over which the Langlands dual group ${\check{{G}}}$ will live. When dealing with the algebraic geometry (as opposed to the topology) of $G$ , we will also view it as living over $F$ ; since $G$ is simply-laced, it is isogenous to ${\check{{G}}}$ .

#### Definition 7.1.

Let $G^{\mathrm{sc}}$ denote the simply-connected cover of $G$ , and let $f\in G^{\mathrm{sc}}$ be a principal nilpotent element as defined in [Ste, Theorem 4.6]. We will denote its image under the map $G^{\mathrm{sc}}\to G$ also by $f$ . Then the map $\mathbf{G}_{a}\to G$ corresponding to $f$ factors through the map $\mathbf{G}_{a}=B\to\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ ; we will denote the image of the standard generator $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 1&1\end{pmatrix}$ under the map $\mathrm{SL}_{2}\to G$ by $e\in G$ . Let $Z_{G}(e)^{\circ}$ be the connected component of the identity in the centralizer of $e$ in $G$ . Define the multiplicative Kostant slice $\mathcal{S}_{\mu}$ by $f\cdot Z_{G}(e)^{\circ}\subseteq G$ . Since $G$ is assumed to be simply-connected, the composite

$$ \mathcal{S}_{\mu}\to G\to G/\!\!/G\cong G/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\cong T/\!\!/W $$

is an isomorphism. We will often denote the inclusion of the Kostant slice by $\kappa:T/\!\!/W\to G$ .

The multiplicative Grothendieck-Springer resolution $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}$ is defined as

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}=B\times^{{\check{{B}}}}{\check{{G}}}, $$

where ${\check{{B}}}$ acts on $B$ by conjugation. (This makes sense thanks to the assumption that $G$ is simply-laced.) There is a natural map $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}\to G$ , given by the conjugation action of ${\check{{G}}}$ on $B$ . Let $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\mu}$ denote the fiber product $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\mu}\times_{G}\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}$ , so that the composite

$$ \widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\mu}\to\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}\to T $$

is an isomorphism; we will denote the inclusion of $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\mu}$ as a map $\kappa:\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\mu}\cong T\to\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}$ .

As with the additive Kostant slice, we will only care about the composite $T\to\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}\to\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}/{\check{{G}}}$ below, so we will also denote it by $\kappa$ . If we identify $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}/{\check{{G}}}\cong B/{\check{{B}}}$ , then the map $\kappa$ admits a simple description: it is the composite $f\cdot T\to B\to B/{\check{{B}}}$ .

#### Definition 7.2.

The stabilizer (inside ${\check{{G}}}$ ) of the multiplicative Kostant slice $\mathcal{S}_{\mu}\subseteq G^{\mathrm{reg}}$ is a closed subgroup scheme of the constant group scheme ${\check{{G}}}\times\mathcal{S}_{\mu}$ , and will be denoted by ${\check{{J}}}_{\mu}$ . It will be called the multiplicative regular centralizer group scheme; if we wish to emphasize the dependence on $G$ , we will denote it by ${\check{{J}}}_{\mu}(G)$ . Note that since the composite $\mathcal{S}_{\mu}\to G^{\mathrm{reg}}\to G/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}$ is an isomorphism, we may identify

$$ {\check{{J}}}_{\mu}\cong\mathcal{S}_{\mu}\times_{G/{\check{{G}}}}\mathcal{S}_{\mu}. $$

Similarly, the stabilizer (inside ${\check{{G}}}$ ) of the multiplicative Kostant slice $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\mu}\subseteq\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ is a closed subgroup scheme of the constant group scheme ${\check{{G}}}\times\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\mu}$ , and will be denoted by $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}$ . Since $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\mu}\cong\mathcal{S}_{\mu}\times_{G}\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}$ , we may identify

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}\cong{\check{{J}}}_{\mu}\times_{\mathcal{S}_{\mu}}\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\mu}\cong(f\cdot T)\times_{B/{\check{{B}}}}(f\cdot T). $$

The following calculation also appears in [BFM], albeit using different techniques.

#### Theorem 7.3.

There is an isomorphism of group schemes over $f\cdot T\cong T\cong\mathcal{M}_{T,0}$ :

$$ \spec(\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}F)\cong(f\cdot T)\times_{B/{\check{{B}}}}(f\cdot T). $$

Just as in Theorem 6.3, the proof of Theorem 7.3 will rely on two lemmas.

#### Lemma 7.4.

The projection map $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}\to f\cdot T$ (onto either factor) is flat.

#### Proof.

Like in the proof of Lemma 6.4, it suffices, by miracle flatness, to show that the fibers of the map $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}\to f\cdot T$ have dimension exactly $\mathrm{rank}({\check{{G}}})$ . The fiber of this map over $f\cdot x\in f\cdot T$ is the scheme

$$ Y=\{(g,y)\in{\check{{B}}}\times T|\mathrm{Ad}_{g}(fy)=fx\}. $$

Observe that the image of $\mathrm{Ad}_{g}(fy)$ and $fx$ (viewed as elements of $B$ ) under the map $B\to T$ are $y$ and $x$ ; so $y=x$ in $T$ , which means that $Y$ is isomorphic to the centralizer $Z_{{\check{{B}}}}(fx)$ . The dimension estimate is equivalent to the claim that $fx$ is a regular element of $G$ , since this means that its centralizer has minimal dimension (namely, the rank of $G$ , which is also the rank of ${\check{{G}}}$ ). The desired regularity of $fx$ follows from the discussion in [Ste, Remark 4.7]. (Note that, as mentioned in loc. cit., the specific choice of the regular unipotent $f$ is crucial for the regularity of $fx$ .) ∎

#### Notation 7.5.

Let $\alpha$ be a root of ${\check{{G}}}$ . Say that a point $x\in T$ is $\alpha$ -generic if $x(h_{\beta})\neq 1$ for all roots $\beta\neq\alpha$ . This implies that the centralizer $Z_{{\check{{G}}}}(x)$ has semisimple rank at most $1$ . Let $T_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}$ denote the $\alpha$ -regular locus. Observe that $T_{\mathrm{reg}}=\bigcup_{\alpha\in\Phi}T_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}\subseteq T$ is open, with complement of codimension $2$ .

The proof of the next result is exactly as in Lemma 6.6.

#### Lemma 7.6.

There is an isomorphism

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}({\check{{G}}})|_{T_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}}\xrightarrow{{\sim}}\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}(Z_{{\check{{G}}}}(x)^{\circ})|_{T_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}}, $$

where $Z_{{\check{{G}}}}(x)$ is the centralizer of some $x\in T_{\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{reg}}$ which lies on the $\alpha$ -hyperplane, and $Z_{{\check{{G}}}}(x)^{\circ}$ denotes the connected component of the identity.

#### Proof of Theorem 7.3.

The argument of Theorem 6.3 reduces us to checking that the isomorphism of Theorem 7.3 holds if $G$ has semisimple rank $1$ , i.e., is the product of a torus with one of $\mathrm{GL}_{2}$ , $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ , or $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ . Again, it is easy to match up the contributions from the toral factors, so we will assume that $G$ is either $\mathrm{GL}_{2}$ , $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ , or $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ . In this case, we can even replace $F$ by $\mathbf{Z}$ .

- • When $G=\mathrm{GL}_{2}$ , we may identify $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}$ with the centralizer (in ${\check{{B}}}$ ) of $\begin{pmatrix}x&0\\ x&y\end{pmatrix}$ . It is easy to compute that $\begin{pmatrix}a&0\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}$ stabilizes $\begin{pmatrix}x&0\\ x&y\end{pmatrix}$ if and only if $c=\frac{a-d}{x-y}\cdot x$ , meaning that

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}\cong\spec\mathbf{Z}[x^{\pm 1},y^{\pm 1},a^{\pm 1},d^{\pm 1},\tfrac{a-d}{x-y}]. $$

The coproduct sends $a\mapsto a\otimes a$ and $d\mapsto d\otimes d$ . The same argument as in Theorem 6.3 implies that

$$ \mathrm{KU}^{T_{c}}_{\ast}(\Omega\mathrm{GL}_{2})\cong\mathbf{Z}[u^{\pm 1},x^{\pm 1},y^{\pm 1},a^{\pm 1},d^{\pm 1},\tfrac{a-d}{x-y}]. $$

The map induced on $T$ -equivariant $\mathrm{KU}$ -homology by the inclusion $T^{2}\to\mathrm{GL}_{2}$ is simply given by the inclusion of the subalgebra $\mathbf{Z}[u^{\pm 1},x^{\pm 1},y^{\pm 1},a^{\pm 1},d^{\pm 1}]$ . The coproduct on this subalgebra (and hence, on $\mathrm{KU}^{T_{c}}_{\ast}(\Omega\mathrm{GL}_{2})$ ) is determined by the formulas $a\mapsto a\otimes a$ and $d\mapsto d\otimes d$ . It follows that $\spec\mathrm{KU}^{T_{c}}_{0}(\Omega\mathrm{GL}_{2})$ is isomorphic to $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}$ as group schemes over $\spec\pi_{0}\mathrm{KU}_{T_{c}}\cong\spec\mathbf{Z}[x^{\pm 1},y^{\pm 1}]$ , as desired.

- • When $G=\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ , we may identify $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}$ with the centralizer (in ${\check{{B}}}\subseteq\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ ) of $\begin{pmatrix}x&0\\ x&x^{-1}\end{pmatrix}$ . An element $\begin{pmatrix}a&0\\ c&1\end{pmatrix}\in{\check{{B}}}\subseteq\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ stabilizes $\begin{pmatrix}x&0\\ x&x^{-1}\end{pmatrix}$ if and only if $c=\frac{a-1}{x-x^{-1}}\cdot x$ . Therefore,

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}\cong\spec\mathbf{Z}[x^{\pm 1},a^{\pm 1},\tfrac{a-1}{x-x^{-1}}]; $$

the coproduct sends $a\mapsto a\otimes a$ . Next, there is an isomorphism

$$ \mathrm{KU}^{S^{1}}_{\ast}(\Omega\mathrm{SL}_{2})\cong\mathbf{Z}[u^{\pm 1},x^{\pm 1},a^{\pm 1},\tfrac{a-1}{x^{2}-1}]. $$

This is proved exactly as in Theorem 6.3; the role of the class $2x$ is now played by the Chern class $x^{2}-1\in\pi_{0}\mathrm{KU}_{S^{1}}$ of the weight $2$ representation of $S^{1}$ . (Recall that the action of $S^{1}$ on $G_{c}\cong\mathrm{SU}(2)\cong S^{3}$ exhibits it as the one-point compactification of the trivial $1$ -dimensional representation summed with the weight $2$ representation of $S^{1}$ on $\mathbf{C}$ .) The map induced on $T$ -equivariant $\mathrm{KU}$ -homology by the inclusion $S^{1}\to\mathrm{SU}(2)$ of the maximal torus is simply given by the inclusion of the subalgebra $\mathbf{Z}[u^{\pm 1},x^{\pm 1},a^{\pm 1}]$ . The coproduct on this subalgebra (and hence, on $\mathrm{KU}^{S^{1}}_{\ast}(\Omega\mathrm{SL}_{2})$ ) is determined by the formula $a\mapsto a\otimes a$ . It follows that $\spec\mathrm{KU}^{S^{1}}_{0}(\Omega\mathrm{SL}_{2})$ is isomorphic to $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}$ as group schemes over $\spec\pi_{0}\mathrm{KU}_{S^{1}}\cong\spec\mathbf{Z}[x^{\pm 1}]$ , as desired.

- • When $G=\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ , we may identify $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}$ with the centralizer (in ${\check{{B}}}\subseteq\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ ) of $\begin{pmatrix}x&0\\ x&1\end{pmatrix}$ . An element $\begin{pmatrix}a&0\\ c&a^{-1}\end{pmatrix}\in{\check{{B}}}\subseteq\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ stabilizes $\begin{pmatrix}x&0\\ x&1\end{pmatrix}$ if and only if $c=\frac{a-a^{-1}}{x-1}\cdot x$ . Therefore,

$$ \widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}\cong\spec\mathbf{Z}[x^{\pm 1},a^{\pm 1},\tfrac{a-a^{-1}}{x-1}]; $$

the coproduct sends $a\mapsto a\otimes a$ . Again, as in the preceding cases, there is an isomorphism

$$ \mathrm{KU}^{S^{1}}_{\ast}(\Omega\mathrm{PGL}_{2})\cong\mathbf{Z}[u^{\pm 1},x^{\pm 1},a^{\pm 1},\tfrac{a-a^{-1}}{x-1}], $$

where the coproduct sends $a\mapsto a\otimes a$ . It follows that $\spec\mathrm{KU}^{S^{1}}_{0}(\Omega\mathrm{PGL}_{2})$ is isomorphic to $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}$ as group schemes over $\spec\pi_{0}\mathrm{KU}_{S^{1}}\cong\spec\mathbf{Z}[x^{\pm 1}]$ , as desired.∎

#### Remark 7.7.

Just for posterity, let us record a more canonical variant of the calculation above for ${\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ , which does not require picking a Borel subgroup (i.e., which does not involve identifying $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}/{\check{{G}}}\cong B/{\check{{B}}}$ ). If $\lambda\in\mathbf{G}_{m}$ , we denote $\lambda+\lambda^{-1}\in\mathbf{A}^{1}$ by $f(\lambda)$ . The Kostant slice $\kappa:{\check{{T}}}\cong\mathbf{G}_{m}\to\widetilde{\mathrm{SL}}_{2}$ is the map sending $\lambda\in\mathbf{G}_{m}$ to the pair $(x,\ell)$ with

$$ x=\begin{pmatrix}f(\lambda)-1&f(\lambda)-2\\
1&1\end{pmatrix},\ \ell=\left[\lambda-1:1\right]. $$

Note that this indeed a well-defined point in $\widetilde{\mathrm{SL}}_{2}$ , since one can check that $x$ preserves $\ell$ : the key point is the conic relation

$$ 2\lambda=f(\lambda)-\sqrt{f(\lambda)^{2}-4}. $$

Indeed, this calculation of $\kappa(\lambda)$ is essentially immediate from the requirement that the following diagram commutes:

$$ \textstyle{\mathbf{G}_{m}\cong{\check{{T}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\kappa} \scriptstyle{\lambda\mapsto f(\lambda)} \textstyle{\widetilde{\mathrm{SL}}_{2}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\mathbf{A}^{1}\cong{\check{{T}}}/\!\!/W\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\kappa} \scriptstyle{\lambda\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}\lambda-1&\lambda-2\\
1&1\end{pmatrix}} \textstyle{\mathrm{SL}_{2}.} $$

Moreover, the $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ -action on $\widetilde{\mathrm{SL}}_{2}$ sends $g\in\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ and $(x,\ell)$ to $(\mathrm{Ad}_{g}(x),g\ell)$ . If $g=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}$ , we directly compute that $\mathrm{Ad}_{g}(x)=x$ if and only if $b=c(f(\lambda)-2)$ and $a-d=(f(\lambda)-2)c$ , in which case $g$ also preserves $\ell$ . Therefore, $g=\begin{pmatrix}(f(\lambda)-2)c+d&(f(\lambda)-2)c\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}$ for $c,d\in k$ . In order for $\mathrm{det}(g)=1$ , we need

$$ d^{2}+c(f(\lambda)-2)(d-c)=1. $$

Both $x$ and $g$ can be simultaneously diagonalized (if $f(\lambda)\neq\pm 2$ ); note that $\lambda+\lambda^{-1}$ is an eigenvalue of $x$ . If $t$ is an eigenvalue of $g$ , then we have $c=\tfrac{t-t^{-1}}{\lambda-\lambda^{-1}}$ and $d=\tfrac{t^{2}\lambda+1}{t(\lambda+1)}$ . When $k$ is not of characteristic $2$ , this shows that

$$ \mathbf{G}_{m}\times_{\widetilde{\mathrm{SL}}_{2}/\mathrm{SL}_{2}}\mathbf{G}_{m}\cong k[\lambda^{\pm 1},t^{\pm 1},\tfrac{t-t^{-1}}{\lambda-\lambda^{-1}}]. $$

This in turn implies that

$$ \mathbf{G}_{m}\times_{\widetilde{\mathrm{SL}}_{2}/\mathrm{PGL}_{2}}\mathbf{G}_{m}\cong k[\lambda^{\pm 1},t^{\pm 2},\tfrac{t^{2}-1}{\lambda-\lambda^{-1}}], $$

as desired.

There is another choice of slice when $G$ is simply-connected; the calculation of Theorem 7.3 continues to hold for it, too, as we now illustrate in the example of $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ .

#### Definition 7.8 (Steinberg slice).

Let $G$ be a simply-connected semisimple algebraic group. Given $w\in W$ , let $N_{w}=N\cap w^{-1}N^{-}w$ , so that $N_{w}=\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi_{w}}U_{\alpha}$ , where $\Phi_{w}$ is the set of roots made negative by $w$ . Let $w=\prod_{\alpha\in\Delta}s_{\alpha}\in W$ be a Coxeter element, and let $\dot{w}$ be a lift of $w$ to $N_{G}(T)$ . Define the Steinberg slice $\Sigma=\dot{w}N_{w}\subseteq G$ . Then [Ste] proved/stated that the composite $\Sigma\to G\to G/\!\!/G\cong T/\!\!/W$ is an isomorphism. Let $\widetilde{\Sigma}$ denote the fiber product $\Sigma\times_{G}\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}$ , so that the composite $\widetilde{\Sigma}\to\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}\to T$ is an isomorphism. We will denote the inclusion of $\widetilde{\Sigma}$ by $\sigma:T\to\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}$ .

#### Observation 7.9.

We will illustrate the calculation of $T\times_{\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}/{\check{{G}}}}T$ (with $T$ mapping to $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}$ by $\sigma$ ) when ${G}=\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ . View a point in $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}$ as a pair $(x\in\mathrm{SL}_{2},\ell\subseteq\mathbf{C}^{2})$ such that $x$ preserves $\ell$ . The Steinberg slice $\sigma:\mathbf{G}_{m}\to\widetilde{\mathrm{SL}}_{2}$ is the map sending $\lambda\in\mathbf{G}_{m}$ to the pair $(x,\ell)$ with

$$ x=\begin{pmatrix}\lambda+\lambda^{-1}&-1\\
1&0\end{pmatrix},\ \ell=\left[\lambda:1\right]. $$

Note that this indeed a well-defined point in $\widetilde{\mathrm{SL}}_{2}$ , since one can check that $x$ preserves $\ell$ . This calculation of $\sigma(\lambda)$ is essentially immediate from the requirement that the following diagram commutes:

$$ \textstyle{\mathbf{G}_{m}\cong{\check{{T}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\sigma} \scriptstyle{\lambda\mapsto\lambda+\lambda^{-1}} \textstyle{\widetilde{\mathrm{SL}}_{2}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\mathbf{A}^{1}\cong{\check{{T}}}/\!\!/W\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\sigma} \scriptstyle{\lambda\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}\lambda&-1\\
1&0\end{pmatrix}} \textstyle{\mathrm{SL}_{2}.} $$

Moreover, the $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ -action on $\widetilde{\mathrm{SL}}_{2}$ sends $g\in\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ and $(x,\ell)$ to $(\mathrm{Ad}_{g}(x),g\ell)$ . If $g=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}$ , one can directly compute that $g$ commutes with $\begin{pmatrix}\lambda+\lambda^{-1}&-1\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix}$ if and only if $a=c(\lambda+\lambda^{-1})+d$ and $b=-c$ . Therefore, $g=\begin{pmatrix}c(\lambda+\lambda^{-1})+d&-c\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}$ for $c,d\in k$ . In order for $\mathrm{det}(g)=1$ , we need

$$ c^{2}+d^{2}+cd(\lambda+\lambda^{-1})=1. $$

As long as $\lambda\neq\pm 1$ , both $x$ and $g$ can be simultaneously diagonalized by $\begin{pmatrix}\lambda&\lambda^{-1}\\ 1&1\end{pmatrix}$ : the diagonalization of $x$ is $\begin{pmatrix}\lambda&0\\ 0&\lambda^{-1}\end{pmatrix}$ , and the diagonalization of $g$ is $\begin{pmatrix}c\lambda+d&0\\ 0&c\lambda^{-1}+d\end{pmatrix}$ . If $t=c\lambda+d$ , then $c\lambda^{-1}+d=t^{-1}$ by the above determinant relation. We also have that $a=t-\tfrac{\lambda(t-t^{-1})}{\lambda-\lambda^{-1}}$ and $c=\tfrac{t-t^{-1}}{\lambda-\lambda^{-1}}$ . This shows that

$$ \mathbf{G}_{m}\times_{\widetilde{\mathrm{SL}}_{2}/\mathrm{SL}_{2}}\mathbf{G}_{m}\cong\spec k[\lambda^{\pm 1},t^{\pm 1},\tfrac{t-t^{-1}}{\lambda-\lambda^{-1}}], $$

and hence that

$$ \mathbf{G}_{m}\times_{\widetilde{\mathrm{SL}}_{2}/\mathrm{PGL}_{2}}\mathbf{G}_{m}\cong\spec k[\lambda^{\pm 1},t^{\pm 2},\tfrac{t^{2}-1}{\lambda-\lambda^{-1}}], $$

as desired.

#### Corollary 7.10.

There is an $F$ -linear equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}F\simeq\QCoh(\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}}). $$

Furthermore, the pushforward functor $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})\to\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\ast;\mathrm{KU})$ identifies with the pullback functor $\kappa^{\ast}:\QCoh(\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}})\to\QCoh(T)$ .

#### Proof.

By definition, $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})$ is equivalent to the category of comodules over $\pi_{0}\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}=\mathrm{KU}_{0}^{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})$ in the category of $\pi_{0}\mathrm{KU}_{T_{c}}$ -modules. By Theorem 7.3, it can be identified the category of quasicoherent sheaves on the quotient stack $(f\cdot T)/\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}$ . We may view $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}$ as a closed subgroup scheme of the constant group scheme ${\check{{B}}}\times(f\cdot T)$ . This gives an isomorphism

$$ (f\cdot T)/\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}\cong{\check{{B}}}\backslash({\check{{B}}}\times(f\cdot T))/\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}. $$

It follows from Steinberg’s work in [Ste] that the ${\check{{B}}}$ -orbit of $f\cdot T$ inside $B$ is precisely the regular locus $B^{\mathrm{reg}}$ . Since $\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}$ is definitionally the stabilizer of $f\cdot T\subseteq B$ , the quotient $({\check{{B}}}\times(f\cdot T))/\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}$ is isomorphic to $B^{\mathrm{reg}}$ ; so there is an isomorphism $(f\cdot T)/\widetilde{{\check{{J}}}}_{\mu}\cong B^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{B}}}$ . To finish, note that $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}}\cong B^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{B}}}$ . ∎

Similarly, there is an $F$ -linear equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{{\check{{T}}}_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}F\simeq\QCoh(\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}^{{}^{\prime},\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}}), $$

where $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}^{{}^{\prime}}$ is ${\check{{G}}}\times^{{\check{{B}}}}{\check{{B}}}$ , with ${\check{{B}}}$ acting on itself by conjugation. Note that $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}^{{}^{\prime},\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}}\cong{\check{{B}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{B}}}$ is an open substack of the stack ${\check{{B}}}/{\check{{B}}}\cong\mathrm{Map}(B\mathbf{Z},B{\check{{B}}})$ of ${\check{{B}}}$ -bundles on the circle $S^{1}=B\mathbf{Z}$ .

The equivalence of Corollary 7.10 is in fact symmetric monoidal for the convolution tensor structure on $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})$ (described in Remark 4.5) and the standard tensor product on $\QCoh(\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}})$ .

#### Remark 7.11.

It can be shown that if $G$ has torsion-free fundamental group, there is an $F$ -linear equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}F\simeq\QCoh(G^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}}). $$

Just as in Section 4, the left-hand side is defined as

$$ \mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})=\mathrm{coLMod}_{\pi_{0}(\mathcal{F}_{G}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee})}(\QCoh(T/\!\!/W)). $$

Note that this is a sensible definition since $\pi_{\ast}\mathcal{F}_{G}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee}$ is concentrated in even degrees. Furthermore, the pushforward functor $\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})\to\mathrm{Loc}_{G_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\ast;\mathrm{KU})$ identifies with the pullback functor $\kappa^{\ast}:\QCoh(G^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}})\to\QCoh(T/\!\!/W)$ . The proof of the displayed equivalence is quite similar to that of Corollary 7.10, and in fact can be deduced from it using the observation that $\pi_{0}(\mathcal{F}_{G}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee})=\pi_{0}(\mathcal{F}_{T}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})^{\vee})^{W}$ and that the natural map $\widetilde{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}\to G^{\mathrm{reg}}$ is a (ramified) $W$ -cover. The first statement uses that $G$ has torsion-free fundamental group, and the second is a multiplicative version of Grothendieck-Springer theory.

In [Dev3, Section 3.7], we study a variant of Corollary 7.10, where $\mathrm{KU}$ is replaced by connective complex K-theory $\mathrm{ku}$ ; that is, $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{KU})$ is replaced by $\mathrm{Loc}_{T_{c}}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{ku})$ .
